paragraphs.text: III. SEVEN BOOKS OF EXPRESSIONS IN THE HEPTATEUCH
BOOK ONE. EXPRESSIONS IN GENESIS
Expressions of the Scriptures that seem to follow the particular usages of the Hebrew or Greek language, which in Greek are called idioms.
And let them divide between the middle of the day and between the middle of the night.

"Birds flying over the earth according to the firmament of heaven." The question is how "according to the firmament" should be understood. The same applies to "Let us make man according to the image and according to the likeness," where many Latin manuscripts have "to the image and likeness."
"Fill the earth and have dominion of it." The Latin idiom, of course, is "have dominion over it."
"And man was not to work the earth": where the Latin manuscripts have "who would work the earth."
"God planted a paradise according to the east": where the Latin manuscripts have "toward the east."

Many Latin manuscripts have "and the tree of knowing good and evil," or "the tree of the knowledge of good and evil," or "the tree of knowing of good and of evil," and there may be other variations among the translators on this point. The Greek has "and the tree for knowing, knowable of good and evil." I do not know whether this is a matter of idiom, or whether it rather suggests some definite meaning.

Where the Latin manuscripts have "of every tree that is in paradise for food you shall eat," the words "for food" are not to be joined to "paradise" but to "you shall eat." For Latin idiom permits one to say "you shall eat with food," since in idioms of this kind it usually puts the ablative, or what they call the seventh case, in place of the Greek dative. Or else the word order is "of every tree for food."
"The serpent was the most prudent of all the beasts," as many Latin manuscripts have it; for the Greek reads φρονιμώτατος ("most prudent"), not σοφώτατος ("most wise").

What is written of Adam and Eve, "their eyes were opened," is an idiom, since it would be absurd to believe that they had previously wandered about in paradise blind or with their eyes shut. The same idiom is used in what is written of Hagar: "she opened her eyes and saw a well"—for she had not been sitting there with her eyes closed before—and in the breaking of bread, when the eyes of those who recognized the Lord after the resurrection were opened; for they had not been walking along the road with him with their eyes closed.

Where many manuscripts have "and I will put enmity between you and between the woman," the Greek has "in the midst of you and in the midst of the woman." This is an idiom, for it means just the same as saying "between you and between the woman." The same holds for what follows: "in the midst of your seed and in the midst of her seed."

Where many Latin manuscripts have "because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate of the tree of which I had commanded you not to eat of it alone," the Greek has "you ate of the tree of which I had commanded you, that alone, not to eat of it." Other Greek translators, however, have "you ate" (using either manducasti or edisti), so that according to them the sense would be: "because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate of the tree of which I had commanded you not to eat that alone, of it you ate."
"And she added to bear his brother Abel." This is a frequent idiom in the scriptures: "he added to say."

"And it came to pass, while they were in the field, Cain rose up against Abel and killed him." This is an idiom. Even without "and it came to pass," the sense could be complete: "and when they were in the field."

Where some Latin manuscripts have "and he repented. And God said: I will blot out man, whom I made, from the face of the earth," the Greek has διενοήθη, which is said to mean "he reconsidered" rather than "he repented." Some Latin manuscripts also have that word.

Most Latin manuscripts have "you shall make nests into the ark," though the Latin idiom would be not "into the ark" but "in the ark." The Greek has neither "into the ark" nor "in the ark" but "you shall make nests the ark," which is understood to mean that the ark itself was to be the nests.
Where most manuscripts have "you shall make the door of the ark from the side," some have "crosswise"; for that is how they chose to translate what in Greek is ἐκ πλαγίων.

Where it is written, "For yet seven days I will bring a flood of water upon the earth," as some Latin manuscripts have it, the Greek reads "I will bring rain upon the earth." The Greek idiom has the genitive case, not the accusative, so that if we rendered it into Latin it would read: "For yet of seven days I will bring rain upon the earth."

What is written, "And Noah did all that the Lord God commanded him, so he did," is an idiom similar to the one in the account of the creation, where after "and so it was done" there is added "and God made."

Where it is written, "I will blot out every raising-up," we should note that it does not say "creation"; for the Greek reads ἀνάστασιν. This noun is also used constantly in the Greek scriptures for the resurrection, though ἐξανάστασις could have been used, so that "raising-up" would be ἀνάστασις and "resurrection" ἐξανάστασις. The apostle used that word: "if somehow I may attain to the resurrection of the dead"; for there the Greek has not ἀνάστασιν but ἐξανάστασιν.

It is written: "And all the beasts according to their kind, and all the cattle according to their kind, and every creeping thing that moves upon the earth according to its kind, and every bird according to its kind went in to Noah into the ark, two by two of all flesh in which (masculine/neuter) is the breath of life." Here "in which" has nothing to refer to unless you supply "kind": that is, "in which kind." For if we supplied "flesh," it would have had to say "in which" in the feminine, as the translator Symmachus alone did.
Where it says again, "and every raising-up was blotted out," we should note that this is an idiom, as if it said "the making" or "creation" of flesh.

Having said, "and every raising-up that was upon the face of all the earth was blotted out, from man to beast, and of creeping things and of the birds of heaven," it then adds, "and they were blotted out from the earth." We should note this idiom of repetition, which scripture uses habitually.

What is written, "He sent out the raven to see whether the water had ceased; and going out it did not return until the water had dried from the earth," is an idiom common in the scriptures, which we should begin to notice right away: for it did not return afterward either, even though it says it did not return until the water had dried up.

What is written, "And he stretched out his hand, took her, and brought her in to himself into the ark," is an idiom which I take to be Hebrew, since it is also very common in the Punic language, in which we find many words that agree with Hebrew. For "and he stretched out the hand" would surely have been enough, even without adding "his." Of the same kind is what it says a little later: "she had an olive leaf, a twig, in her mouth."
"And she did not add to return to him any more": this is a very common idiom in the scriptures.
What is written, "And I will not add any more to curse the earth," is like the earlier "and she did not add to return to him."
"And I will not add to strike all living flesh": the same idiom.
"And indeed your blood of your souls": when either "your blood" or "the blood of your souls" would have been enough.
"This is the sign of the covenant that I set between the midst of me and of you": that is, "between me and you."
"He was a giant hunter against the Lord God." It is uncertain whether this can be understood as "before the Lord God," for that is how the Greek word ἐναντίον is usually understood.
"From where Philistim went out from there": when "from where Philistim went out" would have been enough.
"And all the earth was one lip": what we ordinarily call "one tongue."
"And all the earth was one lip": we should note that "all the earth" here means all the people who were then alive, even though they were not yet spread over all the earth.
"And they had bricks for stone." The Greek has "and they had bricks into stone." If this were said that way in Latin, the idiom would be less readily understood.

"Come, let us build ourselves a city and a tower whose top shall reach to heaven." This is said by hyperbole, if we are to take it here as a figure of speech; but if "to heaven" is taken literally, it should be considered among the questions.

Where some Latin manuscripts have "Shem the son of Noah was a hundred years old when he begot Arphaxad," the Greek has "Shem son of a hundred years when he begot Arphaxad." There is an ellipsis here, since "was" is missing. But that it does not have "son of Noah" but only "son" is a new idiom.
"And Sarai was barren and did not bear": when "and Sarai was barren" could have been enough.
"It will be, then, when the Egyptians see you, they will say that this is his wife." The "that" is added as a matter of idiom, for "this is his wife" would have been enough.
Where scripture says, "And it came to pass, as soon as Abram entered Egypt," it would have been enough to say "And as soon as Abram entered Egypt."

"What is this you have done to me, that you did not announce to me that she is your wife?" when "you did not announce" would have been enough. And "announce" itself is said in the manner of the scriptures; for most Latin manuscripts have "you did not tell."

"And Abram went up out of Egypt, he and his wife and all that was his, and Lot with him, into the desert": "they went up" is understood. Yet what he had that was lifeless, such as gold and silver and all his goods, cannot properly be said to have gone up with him. Hence we recognize here the figure of speech which in Greek is called zeugma [?].

"And there was strife between the midst of the herdsmen of Abram's flocks and between the midst of the herdsmen of Lot's flocks." Almost all the Latin manuscripts did not translate this idiom but put it the way our usage has it. From here on we have decided not to note it either; for it is the same throughout the Greek scripture wherever something of this kind is said.

"For we are men, brothers." Abram says this to Lot. From this we understand that it is the custom of scripture to call members of one family "brothers," even if they differ in degree of kinship, one being in a higher generation and the other in a lower, as here; for Abram was his uncle.

"And it came to pass in the reign of Amraphel king of Shinar." By the custom of our idiom it would have been enough to begin thus: "And in the reign of Amraphel." So when scripture says "and it came to pass," it is speaking in its own manner.
"And in the fourteenth year Chedorlaomer and the kings who with him": "were" is understood, and so some Latin manuscripts have even added it.
"And the Horites who in the mountains of Seir": "were" is understood.

"Now one of those who had escaped, arriving, told Abram the one from across the river—and he was living by the oak of Mamre—of Amor the brother of Eshcol and brother of Aner, who were sworn allies of Abram." This is an obscure hyperbaton. The order is: "One of those who had escaped, one of Amor the brother of Eshcol and brother of Aner, who were sworn allies, arriving, told Abram the one from across the river; and he was living by the oak." The hyperbaton becomes still more obscure through an ellipsis; for after the words "one of Amor the brother of Eshcol and brother of Aner," it does not say what of the brother he was, but "son" is understood. So we say "James of Alphaeus": although "son" is not said, nothing else is understood. And there are many such idioms in the scriptures, where "son" is left unsaid and understood.

Some Latin manuscripts have: "And Abram said to the king of Sodom: I will stretch out my hand to God Most High, who created heaven and earth, if from a cord of esparto to a shoe-strap." The translators were misled because the Greek has σπαρτίου, which in Latin is understood as "thread." And this is an idiom of the scriptures.

"I will stretch out my hand to God Most High, who created heaven and earth, if I take anything of all that is yours." If he said "I will stretch out my hand to God Most High" as if to say "I swear," the idiom is not usual in Latin unless it is put this way: "I stretch out my hand to God Most High that I will not take anything of all that is yours."

"Knowing you shall know that your seed shall be a sojourner in a land": this is indeed a very common idiom of the scriptures; but the Greek has "you shall know, knowing," which comes to almost the same thing.
"And she gave her to Abram her husband, to him, as wife": "to him" is superfluous.

"And when she saw that she had conceived, I was despised before her." The Greek here has a participle that Latin does not have, namely ἰδοῦσα; but if one said, "And seeing that she had conceived, I was despised before her," it sounds almost like a solecism. So too with that participle which is given as [?], for which we have said "seeing."
Where the Latin manuscripts have "I will increase you exceedingly much," the Greek has "exceedingly, exceedingly."

"And I will give to you and to your seed after you the land in which you live, all the land of Canaan, as an eternal possession." We must consider whether it is an idiom when it says "eternal"—the Greek has αἰώνιον—and when it says "and to your seed after you"; for there it meant that what it had said, "to you," should be understood.
"But you shall keep my covenant, you and your seed after you throughout their generations": "you shall keep" for "keep." It has put the promissory mood for the imperative.
"And every masculine one among you shall be circumcised at eight days old": for "every male"—as though anyone but a male could be circumcised.

"And Abraham fell on his face and said in his mind, saying: If to me, a hundred years old, there shall be born, and if Sarah at ninety years shall bear!" There is no doubt that this idiom expresses wonder, not doubt.
"And Abraham was ninety-nine years old when he was circumcised the flesh of his foreskin." It did not say "in the flesh" or "with respect to the flesh."
"And Abraham ran into the cattle." It did not say "to the cattle."
"Now Abraham and Sarah were old, advanced in days": where the Greek has "advanced of days."

"And the Lord said: The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah is filled up, and their sins are very great." Scripture usually speaks of an "outcry" for wickedness so shameless and unrestrained that it is not hidden out of either shame or fear.
"And he said that: I will not destroy it, if I find forty-five there." The "that" seems superfluous, and so it is not found in some Latin manuscripts.
"Lord, surely not, if I speak": "will you be angry" or something of the kind is understood.
"When the Lord overthrew the cities in which he lived in them."
"In every place where we enter, there."

"And God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of living water." This is an idiom, for her eyes had not been closed. We already spoke of it at the beginning of the book, where it is written: "and their eyes were opened."
"And the land which you have inhabited in it."
"And both of them set up a testament," or "both of them made a testament." Scripture likes to call a pact by the name of testament.
"Take your beloved son": "take" is said in the same idiom in which it was also said to Hagar about her son.
"And Abraham, looking back with his eyes": when "looking back" would have been enough.

"By myself I have sworn: unless blessing I will bless you." As if it said, "By myself I have sworn that blessing I will bless you," or simply, with no word added, "By myself I have sworn: blessing I will bless you."
"And multiplying I will multiply your seed": when "I will multiply" could have been enough.
"And it was announced to Abraham, saying (plural)": when the usual way of speaking would be "they announced to Abraham, saying," or "it was announced by people saying."

"And Abraham rose up from his dead": it did not say "from his dead" in the feminine. And again about the same woman: "and I will bury," he says, "my dead." The Greek scripture shows that this is said not in the neuter, as of a dead body, but in the masculine gender.
"And I will adjure you by the Lord God of heaven and God of earth." The Greek does not have "by," but "I will adjure you the Lord God of heaven."
"With whom I live among them."
"Lest perhaps the woman is unwilling to come with me": to call a female, even an unmarried one, a "woman" is peculiar to that language.
"Into the land from which you came out from there."
"Take heed to yourself that you do not take my son back there": words like these are usually used to express a warning.

"And the servant put his hand under Abraham's thigh and swore to him concerning this matter." So it is an idiom when Abraham had said "I adjure you," as if he had said "swear to me"; but we do not usually speak that way. Still, we should watch whether there are other similar idioms in the scriptures. For when Abraham also said, "If the woman is unwilling to come with you, you will be free of this oath," he made it clear that he had said "I adjure you" as though saying "swear to me."

In what is written of Rebekah, "Now the virgin was very beautiful in appearance; she was a virgin, no man had known her," this repetition suggests praise of her virginity. But why "no man had known her" was added, unless it is a matter of idiom, is a wonder—unless it can be understood to mean that "virgin" is a term for her age, not her chastity. The Greek, however, has not "had known" but "knew," which seems not to fit.
"He worshiped to the Lord": where we usually say "he worshiped the Lord."
"For he has not forsaken righteousness and truth from my master": that is, the righteousness and truth that come from my master, as if it said, "which my master has done."
"And the girl ran and told it into her mother's house": as if it were not also her father's house.
"And water to wash his feet and the feet of the men who were with him."
"The Lord, whom I have pleased before him, he himself will send his angel with you": as if "whom I have pleased" were not enough. Or could he please him otherwise than before him?
"If you prosper my way, on which I am now setting out on it."

When Abraham's servant related the words he had spoken as he was about to approach the spring, he related them thus: "And it shall be that the virgin to whom I say, 'Give me a little water from your jar to drink,' and she says to me, 'You drink too, and I will draw for your camels'—this is the woman whom the Lord has prepared for his servant Isaac." These words show clearly enough that in Hebrew idiom those who were virgins were also called women.
"And I blessed the Lord God of my master Abraham." This is an idiom of honor, and very familiar in the scriptures, as in "the God of Elijah."

"Tell me, so that I may turn to the right or to the left." By "the right" he meant success and by "the left" failure: that is, "the right" if they agreed, "the left" if they did not; for he was certainly going to go back by the way he had come. Other passages of the scriptures will also point to this idiom, for "right" is used of all good things and "left" of bad ones, whether happiness and unhappiness or righteousness and unrighteousness, and sometimes "right" of eternal things and "left" of temporal ones.
"These are the names of the sons of Ishmael according to the names of their generations": as if it had said, according to the names by which their generations were called.
"He took Rebekah, daughter of Bethuel the Syrian of Mesopotamia, sister of Laban the Syrian, to himself as wife": when one could have said just "as wife," or "himself a wife."
"And there were twins to her in her womb": when "her" could have been left out.

"And the young men grew." There is an idiom of this kind in secular authors too, as in "and they hide the shields hidden"—that is, by hiding them they make them hidden. So here too, "the young men grew," though they were infants, is understood to mean that by growing they became young men.
Jacob to Esau: "Sell me today your birthright to me"; for this is what the Greek manuscripts have.
"Seeing we have seen that the Lord is with you."

"And we will set up a testament with you." The scriptures like to put "testament" for "pact," that is, διαθήκη. Where the Latin manuscripts have "and we will set up a testament with you, that you do us no harm," it is as though it said: that you may make a pact not to do us harm.
"And he called his elder son Esau and said": here the word "elder" does not mean advanced in age, but older by comparison.

"Now therefore take your vessel, and the quiver and the bow": it did not say "vessels," but "vessel." What he meant us to understand is not clear, unless perhaps it is an idiom, so that by "vessel" he meant the quiver, and to explain what he had called a vessel added "and the quiver and the bow," as if he had said "take your vessel and quiver," that is, "take your vessel, namely the quiver," and then something else, "and the bow," which would not belong to that vessel which is the quiver. Or else he meant to call the quiver and bow together a "vessel," putting the singular number for the plural, as if one said "take your garment," by which word we would understand several garments, just as we understand "the soldier" for soldiers; and there are many other examples.
"Go out into the field and hunt me a hunting."
"And go to the sheep and take me from there two kids, tender and good." By the word "sheep" he meant both kinds of flock, since they were together in the same pastures.
"And may he give you the blessing of your father Abraham": Isaac says this to his son about the son's grandfather, his own father.

"And he went out to Mesopotamia of Syria": as though Mesopotamia could be said to be of anywhere but Syria; although the Seventy are reported not to have "of Syria," but it is written with an asterisk.
God to Jacob: "I will not forsake you until I have done all that I have spoken to you": as though he would abandon him once he had done it. Certainly not; but it is an idiom.
"And Jacob rose from his sleep and said that: The Lord is in this place, and I did not know it." The sense is complete even without "that."
"The Lord is in this place": as if it said, "Here is a manifestation of the Lord"; for the Lord is not in a place.

When Jacob asks, "Do you know Laban the son of Nahor?" although Laban was the son of Bethuel, we should understand that Nahor was the more distinguished, and that it was because of his standing that Jacob asked about Laban by reference to him. To call someone the son of his grandfather or great-grandfather or of some still earlier ancestor from whom he descends is a very common idiom. This is why Isaac too called Abraham the father of his own son, as I noted a little earlier.
"There is still much day; it is not yet the hour for gathering the flocks."
"And she gave him Bilhah her maid, to him as wife": it would be complete even if "to him" were not added.

"If I have found favor before you, I would have divined; for God has blessed me at your coming." This does not seem to follow, since here he should have said, "If I had found favor before you, I would have divined." But as it is, "If I have found" is the right order; that is: "If I have found favor before you, allow me to divine." For he said "I would have divined" as though saying "O, if only I could divine!"—that is, if only I could keep you in my house as a good omen.
"My righteousness will hear me tomorrow": that is, it will cause me to be heard.

"And Jacob saw Laban's face, and behold, it was not toward him as it had been yesterday and the day before": a very common idiom in the scriptures. He used "yesterday and the day before" for time past.
"And I saw with my eyes in sleep," although the body's eyes are closed in sleep.

"I am the God who appeared to you in the place of God": this is an idiom. Or should "God in the place of God" be understood in the same way as "The Lord rained from the Lord," that is, the Son from the Father?
"But Jacob answered and said to Laban: For I said, lest perhaps you take your daughters away from me, and all that is mine."

"And Laban went in and searched in Leah's house": we should notice how the wife's "house" is spoken of, when they had been overtaken by Laban on the road. Perhaps the scriptures customarily say "house" for a chamber or tent, just as they also speak of the maidservants' houses.

Jacob says to Laban: "Since you have searched all the goods of my house": now he speaks of one house, made up of the houses of his wives and concubines. So we are to understand that they were called houses although they were chambers or tents, which are also called pavilions.
"Unless the God of my father Abraham and the Fear of Isaac had been with me": he calls his grandfather his father, just as Isaac his father had spoken to him.

"And Jacob sent messengers before him to Esau his brother, to the land of Seir, into the country of Edom, and he instructed them, saying: Thus shall you say to my lord Esau: Thus says your servant Jacob: I have lived with Laban and have stayed until now; and I have come to have oxen and asses and sheep and menservants and maidservants; and I have sent to tell my lord Esau." He did not say: "I have sent to tell you."

"If Esau asks you, saying: Whose are you? And where are you going? And whose are these things going before you? And you shall say: Your servant Jacob's": it would be full and complete even without the "and."

"He has sent gifts to my lord Esau, and behold, he himself is behind us." In the usual idiom, however, it should have said: "I have sent gifts to my lord, to you," or: "He has sent gifts to his lord, to you."
"He rose that same night and took the two wives and the two maidservants." Here the maidservants are distinguished from the wives, although scripture had earlier called them wives.

"And he took the two wives and the two maidservants": we should note how "took" is used in the customary idiom of the scriptures; for he did not marry them at that time, nor did he receive them then from his father-in-law.

Where the Latin manuscripts have "and the sheep and the cattle are giving birth," the Greek have "are giving birth upon me." This is said in the sense of "upon my concern or care," just as we commonly say that something is "on our head" when it is our heaviest responsibility.

"And Jacob's sons came from the field, and when they heard, the men were pierced to the heart, and it grieved them greatly that he had done a shameful thing in Israel by lying with Jacob's daughter; and it shall not be so." It is hard to find an idiom like this in the scriptures, where the writer inserts the speakers' words without bringing them in as speakers. For he does not say "and they said"; he gives their words while leaving that unsaid. For who else could have said "and it shall not be so" but those who, deeply indignant, were plotting revenge?
We should note that Hamor, speaking about Dinah to Jacob and his sons, says "your daughter," addressing them all; he does not say "your daughter" to Jacob alone and "the sister of these men."
"In this we shall be like you and shall dwell in you," that is, among you.
"For he was attached to Jacob's daughter," that is, he loved her.
"And they killed his son Shechem with the mouth of the sword": as if to say "with the sword."

The things that Jacob's sons carried off from the city of the Shechemites, Salem, when they had taken it by storm, are listed thus: "Their sheep and their oxen and their asses, whatever was in the city and whatever was in the field, they took. And all their bodies <and all their household goods and their wives> they took captive, and they plundered whatever was in the city and whatever was in the houses." Among all these it is not clear enough what he meant by "and their bodies." We must not suppose that they carried off the bodies of the slain. Rather, "bodies" should be understood as things that are possessed in bodily form, so that what follows, "and household goods" and the rest, spells this out, just as in law one speaks of the "delivery of bodies." It is true that the Greeks, in a very common idiom, call slaves "bodies" (sōmata). But since what is written here is not [?] but [?], we should not rashly assert that slaves are meant. Yet this may well be the more likely sense.

When scripture mentions the nation of Edom, that is, of the Idumaeans, and those who reigned in it, it afterward says: "These are the names of the chiefs of Esau according to their places, in their regions and in their nations." It calls them nations although they are one nation, because the families had multiplied over the generations. Esau himself was also called Edom, which is why the nation he founded was named after him; he was, of course, its father.

"When Reuben heard, he delivered him from their hands and said: Let us not strike him in his soul." So he did not first deliver him and then say this; rather, by saying this he delivered him. Thus scripture first said "he delivered him," and then by a brief recapitulation shows how he delivered him.

"Let us not strike him in his soul." In this place the word "soul" means the life of the animate body: what is produced is named after what produces it. In this sense we may also take what was said to the devil about Job: "Do not touch his soul," that is, do not kill him. But it is in the other sense, in which the nature of the soul itself is meant, that the Lord says: "Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul."
When Judah says, "but let our hands not be upon him," this is what we usually express as "let us not lay hands on him."

"For he is our brother and our flesh": this is not something different but the same thing said twice, as though explaining what "our brother" means, namely "our flesh," since they had been begotten of the same flesh.

"They killed a kid of the goats." Scripture often speaks this way, as in the psalm: "like lambs of the sheep." As if there could be a kid that was not of the goats, or lambs that were not of the sheep!
"And it was told to Tamar his daughter-in-law, saying"; but it should have said: "they told her, saying."
"And she put off from herself the garments of her widowhood." What would be lacking if "from herself" were not added?
"And he did not add to know her any more": meaning to have intercourse with her.
"And Joseph found favor in the sight of his master." Everyone knows this idiom in the scriptures.
"And he did not know nothing of what was around him." Among the Greeks this is a common popular idiom; with us it is not correct, and we say instead "he did not know anything."

"Except the bread that he himself ate." By "bread" he clearly wanted us to understand everything that had to do with his food. This is why in the Lord's Prayer bread alone is understood to stand for daily sustenance.
"And his master's wife cast her eyes on Joseph": this idiom is commonly used among us as well, meaning "she loved him."
"And she said: Sleep with me." This too is a common idiom, meaning "lie with me."
"And the keeper of the prison gave the prison through the hand of Joseph": meaning "into Joseph's hands," by which it signifies "into his power."
"And they said: We have seen a dream, and there is no one to interpret it." Although each had seen his own dream, they did not say "we have seen dreams" but "we have seen a dream."

"The three branches are three days"; he did not say "they signify three days." This idiom must be carefully noted, in which things that signify are called by the names of the things they signify. Hence the apostle says: "And the rock was Christ"; he does not say "the rock signified Christ."
"And you will give the cup to Pharaoh into his hand," although it would be complete even without "into his hand."
"And Pharaoh will take your head from you": it would be complete even without "from you."
"And the birds of the sky will eat your flesh from you": an idiom similar to the one above.
"And it came to pass after two years of days": what would be lacking without "of days"?

"And Pharaoh arose, and it was a dream." The scriptures like to speak of dreams this way once the person has woken, as though, when the truth of waking life is given back to him, what had seemed true while it was being seen is then revealed to be a dream.
"I remember my sin today. Pharaoh was angry with his servants and put us in prison": he was speaking to Pharaoh as though about someone else.
"And we both saw a dream in one night, I and he": as if it were not enough to have said "both." Here too he says "we saw a dream," not "we saw dreams," as though both had seen one.

"And it came to pass that as he interpreted for us, so it happened." "And it came to pass": scripture often puts it this way. For it would be complete as: "for as he interpreted for us, so it happened."
"Such as I never saw such in all the land of Egypt uglier": in our way of speaking one could say "than which I never saw uglier," or "such as I never saw," or "I never saw such."
"Rising up, I slept." He says "rising up" for "waking."
"What God is doing he has shown to Pharaoh": though he was speaking to Pharaoh, he speaks as though about someone else.
"And the famine will consume the land": for "the people who are in the land."

"Now therefore look out a prudent and intelligent man and set him over the land of Egypt; and let Pharaoh act and appoint local governors over the land." It is as if the one to whom he said "look out a prudent man" were someone other than the one of whom he says "let Pharaoh appoint."
"And let the wheat be gathered under the hand of Pharaoh": that is, "under his power."

"Only the throne will I go before of you." This is how the words Pharaoh spoke to Joseph run in Greek. "Go before of you" is a usual idiom among the Greeks, whereas we say "go before you." But "go before you the throne" is said not to be usual even among the Greeks; rather they say "go before you in the throne," that is, in the honor of the seat, which is understood as "I will be above you in the kingship." For he says this to him later as well.

"I am Pharaoh; without you no one shall lift up his hand over all the land of Egypt." As if to say: "I am the king, but you are the ruler or governor of Egypt." For Pharaoh is not the name of a man but of royal power.

"And Jacob, seeing that there was selling in Egypt, said to his sons: Why are you idle? Behold, I have heard that there is selling in Egypt": note that what he says he has heard, scripture had said he saw.
"Buy us a little food, that we may live and not die." One of these would suffice: either "that we may live" or "that we may not die."

"We are peaceable; your servants are not spies." They said "your servants are not spies" as if speaking of others, when they could have said "we are not." But they spoke this way chiefly as a mark of respect.

"We your servants are twelve brothers in the land of Canaan," though later they say that one of them is not, because they thought that Joseph was no more, that is, that he had perished. It is by this idiom that scripture also says: "These are the sons of Jacob who were born to him in Mesopotamia," although Benjamin was not born there. And when they said "we are in the land of Canaan," although at the time they were speaking they were in Egypt, "we are" was said for "we live"; for they had come from there and meant to return at once, since they lived there.
"This is what I said to you, saying that you are spies": what would be lacking even if he did not add "saying"?
"But you, go and lead the purchase of your wheat." "Lead" stands for "carry": since the pack animals that carry it are led, the load too is said to be led.
"Did I not speak to you, saying: Do not harm the boy, and you did not hearken to me?" Note that "hearkening" is not used only of God's hearkening.

"But they did not know that Joseph heard." "Heard" stands for "understood"; for even someone who does not understand a language still hears its sounds with his ear. This idiom recurs when they tell their father what happened to them in Egypt and what they said to Joseph.

"We are twelve brothers, sons of our father; one is not, but the youngest with our father today in the land of Canaan." There are many kinds of idiom in these few words. There is the one I mentioned a little earlier, "we are twelve," though they themselves say "one is not." There is "we are sons of our father," as if they could be sons of someone other than their own father. And in "but the youngest with our father today in the land of Canaan" they did not say "is" or anything of the kind. Next we must note something that seems especially necessary because of the evangelists' narratives: when things that were said are reported, they are not repeated in exactly the same way, and yet in the difference of words nothing of the truth of the meaning is lost. For the words they report Joseph as having said to them, "and trade in the land," are not found among the things he said. Yet they were not lying, because they recognized this as his intention from the words he had spoken. Words are needed only to express our intention and to convey it, as far as we can, to the knowledge of those who hear.
"And each one's bundle of silver was in their sack": he did not say "in his sack" or "in their sacks," but spoke as if there were one sack for all of them.
"All these things have come upon me": that is, they weigh me down with misery.
"And Judah said to him, saying": this could have been complete even without "saying."
"Asking, the man asked us." Such an idiom is constant in the scriptures: "asking, the man asked us," or "by asking he asked," and similar expressions.

"For the men will eat loaves with me at midday": surely not only loaves? The idiom takes in everything else under the chief item. "For the men will eat loaves with me at midday": by "at midday" he means the midday meal, which is taken in the middle of the day; for that is what midday is.

"That he may take us as slaves, and our asses." "As slaves" is certainly not to be understood with "our asses"; for where the Latin manuscripts have "slaves," the Greek reads paidas (servants), which asses can in no way be. So with "our asses" only "take" is understood.
"We opened our sacks, and this silver, each one's in his sack": he did not add "was found" or "appeared" or "was" or anything of the kind.
"Gracious to you; do not be afraid." In the words "gracious to you" two words are understood, "be" and "God"; the full form is "May God be gracious to you," which is very common in Greek.
"Your boy, our father, is well; he is still alive." Here it is shown more clearly that the word "boy" usually means a servant; for in that old man it could not be a word for his age.
"For the Egyptians could not eat bread with the Hebrews; for it is an abomination to the Egyptians." This idiom is frequent, by which all foods are understood under "bread."

"And Benjamin's portion was made magnified fivefold beyond the portions of all, compared with theirs": since it had already been said "beyond the portions of all," "compared with theirs" did not need to be said.

"And finding them he said <to them> according to these words." He could have said: "he said these words to them." Or perhaps this is not just a kind of idiom but also affects the meaning? For it is one thing to say the very words, another to speak according to them, so that whatever other words are used, the same meaning is kept that was contained in those words. That is what "according to them" means, even if they are not the same words. But there follows their reply: "Why does my lord speak according to these words?" In the usual way they should surely have said: "Why does my lord speak these words?" So it is clear that this is a kind of idiom.

"Far be it from your boys to act according to this word." They could have said: "far be it from us." But it is a mark of respect, usual in the scriptures, to speak this way, as though of others; and "boys" is said for "slaves."

"And we will be slaves to our lord." Here too the Greek has paides, that is, "boys." Scripture uses this word for slaves so constantly that it is hard to find a place where it does not call slaves by this name.

"How shall I go up to my father if the boy is not with us? That I may not see the evils that will befall my father!" Ordinary usage would rather have required: "that I may see the evils that will befall my father," that is: "How shall I go up, to see them?" So by an unusual way of speaking he said "how" as if he had said "not." For the usual order of these words is: "I will not go up to my father if the boy is not with us, so that I may not see the evils that will befall my father."

When Joseph wept as he made himself known to his brothers, scripture says: "And all the Egyptians heard, and it was heard in Pharaoh's house." Then follows what it was narrating: "And Joseph said to his brothers." So scripture first told what happened later, for it was through the spread of the report that it became known to all the Egyptians; and afterward, by a brief recapitulation, the narrative returned to what was being said.

"And the voice was spread abroad in Pharaoh's house, saying: Joseph's brothers have come." He put "saying" for "of people saying"; for it was the voice of people saying "Joseph's brothers have come" that was spread abroad.
"But he answered, What is it, saying?" The order is: "But he answered, saying: What is it?"
God says to Jacob: "And I will go down with you into Egypt, and I will make you go up at the end." This is what the Greek manuscripts have, where the Latin have: "and I will lead you to the end."
"And he sent Judah before him to Joseph, that he might meet him near the city of Heroum." I do not know whether the name Heroum is readily found in the scriptures.

Joseph says to his brothers: "I will go up and tell Pharaoh, and say to him: My brothers and my father's household, who were in the land of Canaan, have come to me; and the men are shepherds — for they were men who raised livestock — and they have brought their beasts and their sheep and all they have." The words "for they were men who raised livestock" were inserted by the writer in his own person, and he returns to Joseph's words by adding "and they have brought their beasts and all they have." So the order of Joseph's words is: "and the men are shepherds, and they have brought their beasts and their sheep and all they have."
"And Pharaoh said to Jacob: How many the years of the days of your life?" "Are" is understood.

"Small and evil have been the days of the years of my life." "Small" is put for "few"; for the days of one person's life cannot be shorter in their span of hours than those of anyone else. Jacob said this in comparison with the lives of his forefathers; for certainly no one now lives the hundred and thirty years he had already reached.
"Wheat according to body," that is, according to the number of bodies. By "body" it means the number of bodies, and by the number of bodies the number of people.
"And the famine had grown very severe, and the land of Egypt failed." He put "land" for the people who were in the land.
"And all the Egyptians came to Joseph, saying: Give us loaves." By "loaves" it means wheat, an idiom in which what produces something is named by what it produces.

"And the land became to Pharaoh"; he does not say "Pharaoh's." Scripture likes to speak this way, as is said in the psalm: "And I have kept your law. This became to me, because I sought out your statutes." Of the Lord's law he said "this became to me," that is, for my benefit.
"Except the land of the priests only, Joseph did not possess." As if he had said: "except the land of the priests only, Joseph possessed all the land."

"And Joseph laid it down for them as a statute in the land of Egypt to this very day, that they should pay a fifth to Pharaoh." From the words "to this very day" we understand that Pharaoh was the name of royal power. For the Egyptians could not have gone on paying the Pharaoh of that time up to the day when these things were being written, since he was no longer alive.
"And the days of Jacob of the years of his life were": scripture often says "days of years" when it could simply say "years."

Where it is written, "Joseph was told that your father is disturbed," some manuscripts have "is troubled," some "is agitated," and others something else, according to how the Latin translators were able to render what is written in Greek as enochleitai. "Is disturbed" seems the more fitting rendering, because it is commonly said of those who are tossed about by bodily affliction as death draws near. And it is from this too that a crowd (turba) is called ochlos. For a crowd is a disorderly multitude, not like a people, which is called dēmos, nor like the common folk, which is called laos, but like an ochlos, which is called a crowd.

When Jacob blessed his grandsons, the sons of Joseph, he said among other things: "And my name shall be invoked upon them, and the name of my fathers." We should note from this that not only hearkening but also invocation is sometimes used of men rather than of God.
"For this one the firstborn": according to the Greek manuscripts, this lacks "is."

In the blessing of Joseph, Jacob says among other things: "From there he who strengthened Israel." It would be strange if "is" were not understood, so that the full form is: "From there is he who strengthened Israel."

Where it is written, "Joseph told his servants the buriers to bury his father," the Latin language has found no word for the entaphiastai. For they do not bury, that is, commit the bodies of the dead to the earth; in Greek that is not entaphiazein but thapsai. The entaphiastai, then, do what is done to bodies that are to be buried: embalming, drying, wrapping and binding them, a task in which the Egyptians take especially great care. So where it says "they buried," we should understand "they prepared the body"; and where it says "forty days of burial," these should be taken as the days of that preparation. For he was not buried except in the place where he had directed that he be buried.
"Speak in Pharaoh's ears": this is a common idiom in the scriptures.

And Pharaoh said to Joseph: Go down and bury your father. Even if Pharaoh said this through those powerful men whom Joseph had sent with his message, so that they would carry his answer back to Joseph, he certainly said it to no one but Joseph himself. This explains the passage in the Gospel where one of the evangelists says that a centurion came to the Lord and said to him: My servant is lying at home paralyzed; another evangelist, telling the whole story more carefully, relates that he sent friends to the Lord to say this to him. In those friends the centurion himself certainly came, since his will was present in them. Hence the saying: Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me.

They mourned him with a great and grievous mourning. The Latin says literally "they mourned a mourning" (planctum), not "they mourned with a mourning" (planctu). This idiom is not unknown in Latin, as when one says "he served a servitude," "he soldiered a soldiering," and the like.

And he will repay us in full for all the evils that we showed him. The apostle also uses this idiom when he says: Alexander the coppersmith showed me many evils. For "we showed" or "he showed" is said in place of "we did" or "he did."

Accept the iniquity of the servants of your father's God. "Accept the iniquity" is an unusual expression for "pardon," "forgive," or "forget." But I think "accept" is used here as if it meant "accept with equanimity," that is, do not take it with resentment.
And coming to him they said. They did not come a second time; rather, what had already been said is said again. Scripture often does this.
BOOK TWO. EXPRESSIONS IN EXODUS.
And they grew very, very strong.

What does it mean when Scripture says of the midwives, "And they made houses for themselves, because they feared God"? Just before this it was said, "God dealt well with the midwives." The statement that they made houses for themselves by fearing God seems to belong with this, as though God's benefits helped them to make houses for themselves. Are we to understand that they had no houses before? Or does the word refer to wealth, or rather to some adequate means for running a household? It seems similar to what Jacob said after fourteen years of service to his father-in-law, when Laban wanted to keep him on: "Now, then, when shall I too make a house for myself?" For he had said that Laban's flocks had increased under his care, as Laban himself had admitted when he said, "God has blessed me since you came." So when Jacob says, "When shall I too make a house for myself?", we should understand "as you have." That seems to be the force of "I too." So the wage which he then proposes to settle with Laban appears to concern the very making of his own house.
"And let every female live, that one": this is what the Greek has; the Latin lacks "that one."

"Now there was a certain man of the tribe of Levi, and he took for himself one of the daughters of Levi": a wife is meant, and some Latin translators thought that word should even be added. Then follows: "and he had her, and she conceived."
It is hard to know what a "tibin" is, because neither the Greek translator from the Hebrew nor the Latin translator from the Greek translated this word; each simply carried it over as he found it.

"Then Moses was afraid and said: If this word has been spread abroad in this way..." Two things should be noted in this expression: first, the sentence is left hanging and is broken off unfinished; second, "word" is used for "deed."

"And God looked upon the sons of Israel and made himself known to them": "and made himself known" is put for [?]; that is, he did among them the things by which they would understand God's care for them.
"Seeing, I have seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt."

"And Moses said to God: Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh king of Egypt, and that I should lead the sons of Israel out of the land of Egypt? And he said: Because I will be with you." So the Greek has it. The Latin, however, says "And who am I," and does not say "that I shall go" and "that I shall lead out," but "that I should go and lead out." And where the Greek has "And he said: Because I will be with you," it is of course understood that he said it to Moses; but the Latin has added all of this and says, "And God said to Moses."
God tells Moses what he is to say to the sons of Israel: "Visiting, I have visited you and all that has happened to you in Egypt"; the Greek has "With visitation I have visited you."
God says to Moses about the sons of Israel: "And they will hear your voice." The Greek has "And they will heed your voice," since "heeding" is said of a man as well.

Where the Latin has "A woman shall ask of her neighbor and of her lodger vessels of silver and gold and clothing," the Greek has "of her fellow dweller," that is, [?], which some Latin translators have rendered "of her cell-mate."
Moses says: "What if they do not believe me nor heed my voice?"—which the Latin has translated "hear."
The Greek has "Stretch out the hand and take hold of the tail"; the Latin has translated it "your hand" and "its tail."
"And stretching out his hand, he took hold of the tail, and it became a rod in his hand."

"And he said to him: So that they may believe you that the Lord God of their fathers has appeared to you." The Greek does not have "And he said to him," but goes straight on: "so that they may believe you"; that is, these are God's words after the miracle had been performed, as though he were still speaking and were only now completing the sentence. For the order of the words is: "Stretch out the hand and take hold of the tail, so that they may believe you"; but the account of the deed has been inserted, and afterward "so that they may believe you" is supplied.
Where the Latin has "And his hand became leprous like snow," the Greek does not have "leprous," but only "it became like snow."

"But if they do not heed the voice of the first sign": so the Greek has it; the Latin, however, has "your voice of the first sign." Accordingly it also goes on: "they will believe you at the voice of the following sign."
"And the water which you take from the river will be blood upon the dry," or rather "upon what is dry," that is, upon whatever is dry. The Latin said this as "blood upon the earth."
Moses says: "I pray, Lord, I have not been eloquent since yesterday and the day before."

"And you shall take this rod in your hand, with which you shall do the signs with it," when it could have said "with which you shall do the signs," or at any rate "you shall take this rod in your hand and do the signs with it." As it is, both have been said, in the customary idiom of the Scriptures.

"Now after those many days the king of Egypt died. And the Lord said to Moses in Midian: Go, set out for Egypt; for all who were seeking your life are dead." Many kinds of expression are to be noted in these words. First, "Go, set out for Egypt," as though "go" alone or "set out" alone were not enough. Next, "for all who were seeking your life are dead," when Scripture has said only that the king of Egypt died, and earlier it was said of him alone that he sought to kill Moses. Or did he die last, after his other enemies? If so, this is not a matter of idiom but of meaning. Again, "who were seeking your life" is usually said in the Scriptures not only in a bad sense but also in a good one. It is used in a bad sense, as here, also in the Psalms: "Let them be confounded and put to shame who seek my life"; and in a good sense: "Flight has perished from me, and there is no one who seeks out my life"—unless perhaps a difference is held to exist between those who seek and those who seek out, so that the one is to be understood in a bad sense and the other in a good.
"And they spoke to the people, saying: Thus says Pharaoh"—an expression the Latin translator was reluctant to render.

"May God look upon you and judge, because you have made our odor detestable before Pharaoh and before his servants, to give a sword into his hands to kill us." So the Greek has it. But the Latin, which we used to read as the best, says "that you should give a sword in his hands": a solecism committed under no necessity of translation, since it is not in the Greek.

"And I established my covenant with them, so as to give them the land of the Canaanites and the land which they sojourned in, in which also they sojourned in it." So the Greek has it, and it certainly sounds absurd in the Greek language too. Yet so great is the authority of the Seventy translators, who were not reluctant to speak in this way. What if there is a hidden meaning here as well? But if there is none, the idiom itself should be noted, so that when it is found elsewhere it may not hinder the sense or drive us to look for something where nothing is to be looked for.

Where the Latin has "I have heard the groaning of the sons of Israel, how the Egyptians afflict them," the Greek has καταδουλοῦνται αὐτούς, which could be translated "reduce them to slavery"; it cannot be done in one word.
"And Moses spoke thus to the sons of Israel; and they did not heed Moses, because of faintness of spirit and their hard labors." It says "heed," not "hear."
"For I am not eloquent," which Moses said to the Lord: the Greek said ἄλογος, not "unskilled," as it would be with ἀμαθής or ἀπαίδευτος.
"These are Aaron and Moses, to whom God said to them that they should lead the sons of Israel out of the land of Egypt": so the Greek has it.
"Look, I have a thin voice, and how will Pharaoh heed me?" Note that it said "heed," not "hear."
"And Moses and Aaron did as the Lord commanded them; so they did." What would be lacking if "so they did" were not said?

"If Pharaoh speaks to you, saying, Give us a sign or a portent, and you shall say to Aaron your brother: Take the rod." Did not the custom of our own speech, and a certain soundness in it, require it to be said thus: "If Pharaoh speaks to you, saying, Give us a sign or a portent, you shall say to Aaron your brother: Take the rod"? Why then has "and" been added there, unless by some peculiarity of Hebrew idiom? For it is said not to be Greek either.

The Latin translators do not seem to me to have rendered Pharaoh's [?] ("sophists") quite suitably by saying "wise men"; for σοφοί is what wise men are called. The Latin translator could have said "sophists," since there is no way of saying it in Latin; and so we now use this word as a Latin one, just as we say "philosophy" not only in Greek but also in Latin. The most eloquent authors of Latin literature have used the name "sophists."
"And Aaron's rod swallowed up their rods": as if it had said, "Aaron's serpent."
Where it is said of Pharaoh, "Look, he is going out to the water," the Greek has "onto the water."
"Let my people go, that they may serve me in the wilderness; and look, you have not heeded until now." How often "you have heeded" is said, even when it is said to a man!

"And the enchanters of the Egyptians did likewise with their sorceries; and Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he did not heed them, as the Lord had said": for it is the usage of Scripture to say "heeded" even when speaking of a man.

"Let my people go, that they may serve me"—with a plural verb, not a singular. This manner of speaking is hardly ever found except where a single thing consists of many. For "people" is a singular noun, but it consists of many. So too with "Let all the earth worship you," where the verb is plural, because "all the earth" was said in place of "the people who are on the earth."
"Look, I will strike all your borders with frogs." So the Greek has it, in a most elegant expression, so that the frogs themselves are understood as the plague by which the land of Egypt is struck.

"And the river will belch forth frogs; and they will come up and enter into your houses, and into the storerooms of your bedchambers, and onto your beds, and into the houses of your servants and of your people, and in your dough and in your ovens; and the frogs will come up onto you and onto your people and onto your servants." Note that after saying "into your houses" and so on, it kept the accusative case; and where it said "onto" in "onto your beds" and so on, it likewise kept the accusative; but with "in your dough" and "in your ovens" it shifted to the ablative. For the Greek, too, changed the preposition, which the Latin does not change. The Greek has εἰς τοὺς οἴκους [?], "into the houses," but for "in your dough" ἐν τοῖς φυράμασιν [?]. It would be surprising if this were not a matter of meaning rather than idiom: perhaps it means us to understand that the frogs sprang up in the dough and in the ovens, not that they came up or burst in from outside; and since it foretells that the river will belch them forth, that from there they filled everything.

"And Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt and brought up frogs; and the frog was brought up and covered the land." In the repetition there is a shift from plural to singular, for "the frog" is plainly put for a multitude of frogs. Somehow or other, to minds steeped in the custom of speech, what is said in the singular often seems more than what is said in the plural. For example, more is understood when one says "There is soldiery there" than "There are soldiers there," or "There is fish there" than "There are fish there."
"And they gathered them into heaps upon heaps": this repetition signifies a multitude of heaps, and it is a familiar one in the Scriptures.

Where the Latin translators have "Stretch out your rod with your hand and strike the earth"—with "earth" in the ablative, not the accusative—the Greek has "the mound of the earth," if indeed this word correctly translates what is said there: τὸ χῶμα τῆς γῆς.

"And the enchanters did likewise with their sorceries, to bring forth gnats, and they could not." Note that "they did" is said in place of "they tried to do." For certainly if they did likewise, they undoubtedly brought forth gnats; but since what follows is "to bring forth, and they could not," they did not do likewise but tried to do likewise. Or else, if perhaps they too, though working by sorcery, nonetheless stretched out a rod in the same manner of action—which Scripture has not stated—then "they did likewise" is to be referred to that.
"And on the land which they are upon, upon it."
"And on that day I will make glorious the land of Goshen, in which my people are, upon it."

"And Moses said: I will go out from you and pray to God, and the dog-fly will go away from Pharaoh and from his servants": as though he were speaking to one person in saying "I will go out from you," and then went on to speak of Pharaoh as another person, from whom the dog-fly was to go away.
"Let my people go, that they may serve me"—with a plural verb.
"Look, at this hour tomorrow I will rain down very heavy hail." "And the hail was very, very heavy."

"And the voices and the hail will cease." Note that Scripture usually calls thunder "voices"; Pharaoh too had called them the voices of God earlier, when he said, "Pray to the Lord for me, that the voices of God may cease," where there is also the idiom that it did not use a plural verb with "voices."

"That you may tell in the ears of your sons and of your sons' sons all the ways I made sport of the Egyptians." Note how "I made sport of" is said, in case it is meant in the same way as "this dragon, which you formed to make sport of it," and that passage in Job: "This is the beginning of the Lord's handiwork, which he made to be mocked by his angels."

"Look, at this hour tomorrow I will bring in much locust." See how it said "frog" above, where we remarked that more is generally understood when something of this kind is said in the singular than if it were said in the plural. For it is plain that "much locust" sounds like more than if it said "many locusts."
"But who, and who, are they that will go?" In more familiar everyday usage we say, "Just who and who will go?"
"There was not left nothing green on the trees." In the manner of our own speech it should have been said: "There was not left anything green on the trees."

Pharaoh to Moses: "I have sinned before the Lord your God and against you; so receive my offense." Joseph's brothers used this expression with him too, when they said, "Receive the iniquity of the servants of the God of your father."
Where the Latin translators have "And no one saw his brother for three days," the Greek has "And no one did not see his brother." Note also that any man at all is called the "brother" of another.

Pharaoh says to Moses and Aaron: "Go and serve the Lord your God; except the sheep and oxen leave." So the Greek has it. It is a very unusual expression, unless a pause is placed before "leave" and "these" is understood, so that the sense is: "Go, except for the sheep and oxen, and leave these." For such an ellipsis frequently occurs in the expressions of the Scriptures.
"And we will not leave a hoof": as though a hoof could remain behind once the cattle had been led away. For what else does "we will not leave a hoof" mean but "we will not leave even a hoof"?
Pharaoh to Moses: "Take heed to yourself to add any more to see my face," in place of: "Take heed to yourself that you do not see my face any more."
"And let every man ask of his neighbor, and every woman of her neighbor, vessels of silver and gold and clothing." Note that the Egyptians are called neighbors of the Hebrews.

"And there will be a great cry throughout all the land of Egypt, such as there has not been, and such as will not be added again. But among the sons of Israel a dog will not mutter with its tongue, from man to beast." This is a most elegant expression. By the dog it indicated the very least of either men or beasts, thus making plain how great a quiet there would be among the Hebrews while the Egyptians were crying out in their bitter bereavement.

"Let them each take a sheep, by the houses of their fatherhoods." It is not easy to understand what it means by "fatherhoods": whether the towns in which they dwelt together, or rather large families descended, as it were, from the fatherhood of each one; for this is said to be what the Greek more nearly signifies.

"But if those in the house are few, so that they are not sufficient for a sheep"—that is, so that their very fewness is not sufficient to consume a sheep—"he shall take with him his neighbor who is near him," that is, the household itself shall take in a neighbor. It has put the near man for men, the singular for the plural—for not one is meant, but as many as are enough. When Scripture was speaking about consuming the sheep, it said, "according to the number of souls, each as much as suffices for him"—"souls" for men, the whole by a part.

"They shall take some of the blood and put it on the two doorposts and on the lintel in the houses in which they will eat them in them." Having said "in which," it said "in them" as well, in a very common way. But with "they will eat them" the question arises, what things are meant, and "meats" is understood. For there follows: "and they shall eat the meats that night, roasted with fire"—where the Latin manuscripts have "who shall eat the meat"; but the Greek manuscripts have κρέα, that is, "meats," though in the neuter gender, and so the Greek reads "in the houses in which they will eat them in them" with a neuter pronoun. This idiom, by which it said "them" before indicating what in the following words would be understood by "them," is like the one we explained concerning Moses' son when the angel wanted to kill him, where we adduced an example from the Psalm: "Its foundations are on the holy mountains; the Lord loves the gates of Zion"—for we do not understand whose foundations they are except from what follows. So here too, "in which they will eat them in them," that is, in which houses they will eat them, is understood of the meats, of which it speaks in what follows.

"And you shall take for yourselves a bundle of hyssop and dip it in some of the blood that is by the door, and you shall smear some of the blood on the lintel and on both doorposts." Here too "a bundle of hyssop" certainly signifies several bundles, just as "frog" means many frogs and "locust" many locusts. When this figure is used with things we do not usually speak of in that way, it causes obscurity.

"And it shall be, when your sons say to you, What is this service? and you shall say to them: This is the sacrifice of the Passover to the Lord." Even without "and," "you shall say to them" would be complete.
"And the sons of Israel went and did as the Lord had commanded Moses and Aaron; so they did." It would not add "so they did" if this were not the custom of the Scriptures.
"And it came about on that day, the Lord brought the sons of Israel out of the land of Egypt."
"And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying."

"Everything that opens the womb, the males." It has brought in the plural after the singular, because the very thing said, "everything that opens," is of course understood not of one but of many. A similar expression is "Give heed, my people," with a plural verb. Of the same kind is what follows shortly after: "Everything that opens the womb among the herds and among the flocks, whatever things are born to you." "Everything ... whatever things are born to you" is the same mode of expression.

"Everything that opens the womb of a she-ass." The Greek has "of a he-ass," by that idiom—which we have already noted in Genesis—in which the masculine is used for the feminine, where Scripture says of Sarah's death, "Abraham, rising from his dead" (masculine), and "that I may bury my dead" (masculine); and such things are often said there of the dead woman.
"For this reason I sacrifice to the Lord everything that opens the womb, the males": an expression like the one above.
"And it shall be for a sign upon your hand," that is, upon your works: where perhaps it is more a matter of meaning than of idiom.
"And the Lord shook off the Egyptians into the midst of the sea." The Greek has "And the Lord shook off the Egyptians the midst of the sea."
"And Israel saw the great hand which the Lord had done to the Egyptians."
"Then Moses and the sons of Israel sang this song to the Lord, and they said to say"; for so the Greek has it: καὶ εἶπαν λέγειν [?].
"And they did not find water to drink." It could have done without "to drink."
"And the people murmured against Moses, saying"—not with a singular participle, but a plural one; for a people consists of many.
"And all the congregation of the sons of Israel came into the wilderness": it did not use a singular verb, because a congregation consists of many.
"All the congregation of the sons of Israel were murmuring against Moses and Aaron": this too is the same idiom.

"And the Lord said to Moses: Look, I will rain down breads on you from heaven." Being about to rain down manna, he promised breads. It is an idiom in which bread is put for food; and Scripture likes to say "breads" in the plural rather than "bread" in the singular.

"In the morning," he says, "you will see the glory of the Lord, when he heeds your murmuring upon God," that is, because you murmur upon God, which amounts to saying "against God." Next, note that in a new way "heeding" is used here not of people praying but of people murmuring, though Scripture certainly rebukes murmuring. It is as though it meant that God knew of their murmuring, and called God's very knowledge "heeding."

"Come near before God, for he has heeded your murmur." Again it uses "heeding" not of prayers and petitions, but even of the murmur of the wicked. God says this later too: "I have heeded the murmur of the sons of Israel."

"And look, on the face of the wilderness, something fine like coriander seed." Since God so often says "the face of the earth," as here "the face of the wilderness," it is astonishing how people can go so wrong, when they hear "face," as to imagine something like the face of a man or of some living creature.

"According to the number of your souls; each of you gather with those who dwell with you." How often Scripture calls men "souls," the whole by a part—but it does not readily use "fleshes" for men, though it does use "flesh," as in "I will not fear what flesh can do to me," which in the same Psalm it says more plainly: "What can man do to me?" Yet it would not say "according to the number of your fleshes," as it said "according to the number of your souls."
"And they gathered it morning by morning": just as "wells upon wells" and "heaps upon heaps," so "morning by morning" is said.
"Let none of you go out, each from his place, on the seventh day": the inserted "each" could also have been left unsaid.
"But there was no water for the people to drink," that is, for drinking.
"And the people reviled at Moses," that is, assailed Moses with curses—that is, they reviled him; for he himself says this in what follows: "Why do you revile me?"
"And the people were murmuring at Moses, saying"—with a plural participle.
"And take in your hand the rod in which you struck the river." It said "in which you struck" in place of what we say, "with which you struck," and this idiom is very frequent in the Scriptures.

"And Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, took burnt offerings and sacrifices for God": "took" stands for "offered." Or is this perhaps a matter of sense rather than idiom, so that he is understood to have taken what Moses had offered? Yet we do not read earlier that Moses sacrificed, nor Aaron, nor any of the Hebrews who were brought out of the land of Egypt. It was only written earlier that Moses set up an altar and called it "The Lord is my refuge." This Jethro, however, we read was the priest of Midian, that is, of the nation of Midian. And it would be strange if Moses began to sacrifice on his arrival, and not rather Jethro himself, who was already a priest.
"Heavy for you this matter": "is" is understood.
"And you shall show them the ways in which they will walk in them."

"But the heavy matters they referred upon Moses"; for so the Greek has it, which the Latins translated "to Moses." Indeed, by that very idiom, "upon Moses," the responsibility is also signified, as though a burden were being shown to have been laid on him. And "heavy word" is said for "heavy question." Hence it continues: "but every light word they judged themselves."

What the Greek has, ἐπονομάσω [?], is expressed more precisely by "I shall name over" (supernominauero) or "I shall name in addition" (adnominauero); some have translated it with the more usual "I shall surname" (cognominauero). But "I shall surname" does not carry the required meaning; still, "I shall surname" comes closer than "I shall name" (nominauero), for some translators said that too.

"And I will come to you and bless you." Although above he spoke in the plural, "you shall make" and "you shall sacrifice," he says "I will come to you" (singular) as if to Israel itself, that is, to the people.

"And these are the ordinances which you shall set before them. If you buy a Hebrew slave," and so on. The idiom should be noted: although the first part was said to Moses, namely "these are the ordinances which you shall set before them," the rest is addressed as much to the people itself as to Moses: "If you buy a Hebrew slave." For this was not said to Moses; rather, what Moses was to say to the people, God was saying as if to the people alone.

"His master shall pierce his ear with an awl, and he shall serve him forever" or "for eternity," where the Greek has εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα. See how in many places Scripture, following this Greek word, says "everlasting" or "eternal" where that eternity is not meant by which eternal things are promised to us, or by which, conversely, the wicked will burn in eternal fire! For this slave, who could not live for eternity, could not serve for eternity; rather, "eternal" is understood to be said of that whose time has no set end. Or else something eternal is certainly signified by this sacred sign.
"I will give you a place to which he who has killed may flee there."
"If anyone strikes his male or female slave in a rod": that is, "with a rod."

"The bull shall be stoned with stones": as if it could be stoned with anything but stones. This idiom differs somewhat from the one by which, in the manner of the Scriptures, it might say "he shall be stoned with stoning," but it is nevertheless similar.
"But if the bull was given to goring before yesterday and the day before": for past time he put a part for the whole, however long that time had been, in the manner of the Scriptures.

"But if anyone opens a pit or digs a pit and does not cover it, and a calf or a donkey falls into it, the owner of the pit shall make restitution." This idiom too is to be understood as the whole meant by a part; for if a horse or a sheep falls into the pit, he is not therefore excused from restitution because this is not written.
"But what has died shall be to him," for "shall be his."
"But if anyone grazes a field or vineyard and lets his livestock graze another field," that is, "someone else's."

"But if you take your neighbor's garment in pledge, you shall return it to him before sunset." He put the genus for the species: it is said as though of anyone who gives any garment at all in pledge, although Scripture shows from what follows that it is speaking specifically of the one who has no garment other than the one with which he covers himself at night.

"And behold, I send my angel before your face, to guard you on the way, to bring you into the land which I have prepared for you. Take heed to yourself and hearken to him." God commands that his angel be "hearkened to" by the people, not of course as one who makes a request, but as one who gives commands.

"And I will send hornets before you, and it will drive out the Amorites": he shifts from the plural to the singular number. What is meant is: the hornet will drive out the Amorites, as one says "the frog" or "the locust"—not because there is only one, but because the plural number is understood through the singular.
"Part by part I will drive them out from before you."
"You shall not make a covenant with them and their gods; and they shall not dwell in your land, lest they make you sin toward me": he did not say "against me," yet it means the same.
"And all the people answered with one voice, they saying."
"And they saw the place where the God of Israel had stood there." "Where he had stood" could suffice, but these are called Hebrew idioms.
"And you shall gild them with gold." The idiom is similar to "he shall be stoned with stones."
"Cups in which they shall offer sacrifice in them."

"Two bases for one pillar on both its sides, and two bases for one pillar on both its sides." Rather than speaking of all of them, he speaks of two, doubling in his usual way, as in "wells, wells," "heaps, heaps," "generations and generations," and the like.
"And you shall gild the pillars with gold, and you shall gild the bars with gold."
"And you shall bronze them with bronze": this idiom is like "you shall gild with gold."

"Outside the veil which is over the testimony": he says this when speaking of the lamp to be lit, meaning that it would be lit outside, where the holy place is, not within the veil which is over the testimony, that is, the holy of holies. So he did not say "over" as though it were a roof or a vault or the firmament of heaven or the lid of the ark; rather he said "over" even of something set in front as a wall would be, just as we say that someone reclines or stands "above" another, certainly not meaning that one is carried by the other.
"An everlasting statute for your generations": "everlasting" in the sense in which we have spoken of many things above.

"And Aaron shall bear the names of the sons of Israel on the oracle of judgment, on his breast, to the one entering the holy place." It would have followed to say "entering the holy place," that is, "Aaron, entering, shall bear," which is how some Latin translators rendered it to avoid a solecism. But since the Greek has "to the one entering" and some Latin versions agree, I thought the idiom should be noted rather than corrected.

"And you shall put on the oracle of judgment chained fringes." Here too some Latin translators, guarding against a solecism, rendered "chained" in the feminine (catenatas) to agree with "fringes"; but the Greek has τοὺς κροσσοὺς τὰ ἁλυσιδωτά [?], with "chained" in the neuter. We usually call this an absolute idiom, when a neuter is attached to a masculine or feminine noun, as if we were to say, "Earthly justices are not stable things."

"And when Aaron begins to perform the priesthood, his voice will be heard to the one entering the holy place in the sight of the Lord and going out." By "his voice" he means the sound of the bells, which is rather his sound. "To the one entering" and "going out" is put for "of the one entering and going out": he put the dative for the genitive.
"And the two kidneys and the fat which over them": "is" is understood, and some translators added it.
"And you shall separate it with a separation."
