"And when Aaron lights the lamps, late he shall burn incense on it." He said "late" for "in the evening," and so the idiom should be noted; for the Greek has ὀψέ. But "late" is not properly said except when the time in which something ought to have been done has passed, so that it is said to have been done late.

"If you take a census of the sons of Israel in their visitation, and each shall give a ransom for his soul to the Lord, and there shall be no ruin among them in their visitation, and this is what they shall give you." This sentence is left hanging because a copulative conjunction is inserted; if it were not inserted, it would not hang. It is placed in three places, and removing it from any one of them makes the sentence complete. Thus, where it says, "If you take a census of the sons of Israel in their visitation, and each shall give a ransom for his soul to the Lord": if it had not said "and they shall give" but only "they shall give," the sentence would be completed and would not hang. For it would then read: "If you take a census of the sons of Israel in their visitation, each shall give a ransom for his soul to the Lord." But if the conjunction is kept here, it must be removed further down, so that it reads: "If you take a census of the sons of Israel in their visitation, and each shall give a ransom for his soul to the Lord, and there shall be no ruin among them in their visitation, this is what they shall give." Or else in the middle, where it says "and there shall be no ruin among them": if you remove the conjunction, the sentence will not hang, for the sense will be: "If you take a census of the sons of Israel in their visitation, and each shall give a ransom for his soul to the Lord, there shall be no ruin among them." But since the same conjunction is placed everywhere, it makes the sentence hang; that is why we thought it should be noted.

"The people rose up against Aaron, and they said to him." This is a common idiom, since a people consists of many. Next, it should be noted that the whole is put for the part. For the apostle, as was in fact the case, said that some of them did this, not the whole people, where he says: "Nor let us serve idols, as some of them did."

"Rise up and make us gods who will go before us." Were they speaking to someone seated? Or should we rather note an idiom here, the one by which it is often said: "Rise up, O Lord," or "Arise, O God, judge the earth"?
"And now let me be, and angered with anger": like "he shall die by death"; Scripture loves to speak this way.
"Whoever has golden things, take them off": he did not say what golden things. Hence Latin translators said: "Whoever has gold, let him take it off."
"Who is for the Lord? Let him come to me."

"They made themselves gods of gold": of one calf. So he put the plural number for the singular. From this too comes the saying: "These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt." Such idioms, in which the plural is put for the singular, are not found, however, except in the kind of thing that could also be done or understood of several. For although that calf was one, more could still have been made, and it was still like many idols. By this idiom it is said that the robbers insulted the Lord, although Scripture testifies that one of them did so; but he was not the only robber. Moreover, when this idiom is used with proper names—which we have not yet found done in the Scriptures—several persons are understood there, as some have spoken of "Phaedras" and "Medeas," though there was one Phaedra and one Medea; but they called "Phaedras" and "Medeas" all who were like Phaedra and Medea. So these idioms are not introduced without reason, nor haphazardly and at random, as the unskilled do by mistake, but in a definite way and by definite rules.

"Go, go up from here, you and your people, whom you brought out of the land of Egypt": the plural "whom" (quos), not the singular "which" (quem). This is so customary that it is rarely said otherwise.

"And the Lord said: Put off the robes of your glories and your adornment, and I will show what I am going to do to you." He ended the sentence by moving from the plural to the singular "you," because they were many and they were one people, as he had said to them: "You are a stiff-necked people." He did not say "thou people" in the singular but "you people," although "you" (uos) is plural and "people" is singular.

"If I have found favor in your sight, let my Lord go with us": as if he were speaking of someone else. These idioms are frequent, but when this is said to God, people think it is said to the Father about the Son. Yet when such things were said to Pharaoh and to Joseph and to others in many places, it was understood as a manner of speaking.
"Lest you make a covenant with those who sit upon the land": as if to say "who have their seats," that is, "who dwell."

"And you shall not make molten gods for yourself." This idiom signifies the whole by a part; for because he named only molten gods, he did not thereby permit carved, hammered, or clay ones to be made, or any kind of image, or manufactured gods of any sort whatever.
"Everything that opens the womb, to me, males." That is: everything that opens the womb shall be mine, of those that are male.

"The firstborn of a beast of burden you shall redeem with a sheep." This too is the whole meant by a part; for if some animal whose flesh is rejected as unclean is not a beast of burden, it is not therefore exempt from redemption, or to be redeemed with anything other than a sheep.
"You shall not slay the blood of my sacrifices over leaven": the idiom is surely "you shall slay the blood" for "you shall shed it by slaying."

"And the sacrifice of the feast of Passover shall not sleep until morning." He said "shall sleep" for "shall remain"; for how will the flesh of a slaughtered and cooked animal sleep? So when it is said, "Why do you sleep, O Lord?" it is said and understood by this kind of idiom: "Why are you inactive?"—that is, "Why do you not avenge?"
Of Moses' forty-day fast Scripture speaks thus: "He did not eat bread and did not drink water." This is the whole meant by a part: by bread it signifies all food, and by water all drink.
"Cut for yourself two stone tablets like the first ones too": "were" is understood. Hence our translators thought this word should actually be added, since such an ellipsis is unusual in Latin.
"And Moses said to all the congregation of the sons of Israel, saying": it would be complete even without "saying."
"And they brought, each one, what their heart brought." It could more usually have been said: "And each one brought what his heart brought."
"And those to whom it seemed good to their soul brought an offering to the Lord": he did not say, "and as it seemed good to their soul."
"And everyone with whom was found ram skins dyed red": which would usually be said, "And all with whom were found ram skins dyed red."
"Everyone bringing an offering, silver and bronze, they brought offerings to the Lord." It would be more usual to say "everyone brought" than "everyone they brought."
"And those with whom was found with them wood that does not rot": "with them" is added in the manner of the Scriptures; for without it the sentence would be complete.

"And every woman wise in mind to spin with her hands." As if one could spin other than with the hands! And "wise to spin" is an elegant and unusual idiom. Then: "every woman they brought": in the manner of the earlier examples, the singular is completed with a plural, since "every woman brought" would be more usual.
"And all the women to whom it seemed good in their understanding spun goats' hair in wisdom." Note that Scripture often calls skill in these crafts "wisdom," that is, σοφία.

"And compositions and the oil of anointing and the composition of incense": we should not understand some other compositions besides these. Rather, having said "and compositions," he added nothing further by the copulative conjunction but explained what he had said, so that we might know which compositions: "and the oil," he says, "of anointing and the composition of incense." He calls them compositions because they were made of many ingredients.

"And every man and woman whose understanding brought them to come and do every work whatever that the Lord commanded to be done through Moses, the sons of Israel brought an offering to the Lord." So "every man and woman" are understood to be the sons of Israel. The other idioms are similar to those above.

"To make gold and silver and bronze": meaning to make things from gold and silver and bronze; for they were not making gold, but things from gold. Similar is what he says a little later: "and to work wood," that is, to make things from wood.

"To do all the works of the holy, to weave woven and varied things with scarlet and fine linen, to do every architectural work of variegation." See, he calls even work in woven materials architectural—surely because they were being made for the tabernacle, which was like a building and was erected like a house. But what he means by "works of the holy" is not clear: whether of the holy priest, since these things are also said of his robe or robes; or of the holy God, for whose worship these things were made; or "works of the holy place," as people spoke of "the holy place" and "the holy of holies."

"Shoulder-pieces holding together on both sides of it": he did not say "of them," although he had said "shoulder-pieces," not "shoulder-piece," as he usually does. For he called the single shoulder-piece by the plural, "shoulder-pieces," just as he speaks of a robe and likewise of "robes."

"And Eliab son of Ahisamach of the tribe of Dan, who architected woven, sewn and multicolored things, to weave with scarlet and fine linen." It is a new usage to say that woven things are "architected." Also, "to weave with scarlet and fine linen" must be understood as the whole meant by a part: from these we understand the rest as well, namely purple and violet.
"And the sons of Israel did as the Lord commanded Moses; so they did": it would be complete even without the addition "so they did."
"And Moses did all that the Lord commanded him; so he did": in the same way as it was said of the sons of Israel.
BOOK THREE. EXPRESSIONS IN LEVITICUS.

"A man of you, if he offers gifts to the Lord from the livestock, from the oxen and from the sheep you shall offer"; that is: if you offer from the livestock, you shall offer from the oxen and from the sheep. Under the name "sheep" he has also included the goat kind, as he usually does in other places too.
"And you shall break them into fragments"; that is: by breaking them you shall make them fragments.
"And his sin that he sinned in it becomes known to him." Two forms of expression are to be noted here: "he sinned a sin", and the addition "in it". For in what, if not in the sin itself?

"But if a soul sins, and hears the voice of an oath, and he himself was a witness, or saw, or knew of it, if he does not report it, and he shall receive sin." The "and" seems to be superfluous; for if it is removed, "he shall receive sin" follows smoothly.

"But if a soul sins, and hears the voice of an oath, and he himself was a witness, or saw, or knew of it, if he does not report it." "And" is put for "that is"; for in the usage of our own speech it could be said like this: "But if a soul sins, that is, hears the voice of an oath," and so on.

"Or touches any of a man's uncleanness, any uncleanness of his by which, if he touches it, he is defiled, and it escaped his notice, but afterward he comes to know it and has offended"; whereas in the correct order it should have said: "and has offended, but afterward comes to know it."

"A soul, if it escapes him through forgetfulness and he sins unwillingly." He does not say "if it escapes her", since he puts "soul" for "person", as he does in other places too, where he first says "soul", which is of the feminine gender, and afterwards brings in the masculine gender, referring to the person. But here this expression is much more compressed, since both genders are placed in immediate succession, so that it says: "a soul, if it escapes him".

This expression alarmed the Latin translators, and they were unwilling to render it, but put it this way: "if any soul is hidden and sins unwillingly"; whereas it is surely one thing for a soul to be hidden and another for something to be hidden from a soul. Yet this is what Scripture says: "if it is hidden from her", not "if she herself is hidden". In another Greek copy, however, we find: "a soul, if it escapes her through forgetfulness"; but even this copy, in what follows, brought in the masculine, saying: "the priest shall make supplication for him, and it shall be forgiven him", for there it has autō. From this it appears that the copyist feared a solecism and yet could not keep to the feminine gender, overcome by the plain evidence of the scripture that follows.

"This is the burnt offering upon its burning on the altar all night until morning, and the fire of the altar shall burn upon it." It could have been without "and", and so read: "all night until morning the fire of the altar shall burn." But the addition of this conjunction creates obscurity for those who are not accustomed to such expressions of the Scriptures.
"This is the law of the sacrifice which the sons of Aaron, the priests, shall offer it before the Lord." Nothing would be lacking if it did not have "it".
"The holy things of holies is." The Greek has it so too; but it is a Greek idiom, which some of our translators, unwilling to render it, gave as: "The holy things of holies are."
"They shall slaughter the ram which for the offense before the Lord." The Latin translators added "is" and said: "which is for the offense"; the Greek does not have this.

"And if he sacrifices his gift as a vow or a freewill offering, on whatever day he offers the sacrifice, it shall be eaten on tomorrow's day"; in place of "on the following day". Hence others have translated it "on the next day".

"Cook the meat in the court of the tabernacle of the testimony in a holy place, and there you shall eat it, and the loaves that are in the basket of consecration, as it was commanded me, saying: Aaron and his sons shall eat them." Some, unwilling to render this expression, said: "as he commanded me, saying", because this seems consistent, whereas the former is a solecism in the usage of our speech.
"And at the door of the tabernacle of the testimony you shall sit seven days, day and night"; in place of "you shall dwell".

"And Moses said to Aaron: Approach the altar, and make your offering for sin and your burnt offering, and make supplication for yourself and your house, and make the gifts of the people and make supplication for them, as the Lord commanded Moses." He does not say "as the Lord commanded me", but speaks as though Moses, whom the Lord commanded, were one person, and the one who was saying this to Aaron were another.

"And the Lord spoke to Aaron, saying: Wine and strong drink you shall not drink," and so on. He concludes this speech of the Lord thus: "all the ordinances which the Lord spoke to them by the hand of Moses." Although it was the Lord speaking, he did not say "which I spoke to them by the hand of Moses", but used the same expression that Moses himself used above.

"An everlasting ordinance throughout your generations, to distinguish between the clean and the defiled," and so on. It is to be noted how he says "everlasting" of what certainly will not be without end.

Moses, speaking to Aaron and to Eleazar and Ithamar his sons, says this too among other things: "From the sacrifices of peace offerings of the children of Israel, the shoulder of removal and the breast of separation, upon the offerings of fat, they shall offer as a separation, to separate it before the Lord. And it shall be for you and your sons and your daughters with you an everlasting ordinance"; although all this was going to come to an end.

When he was giving commands about the living creatures that are in the waters, which of them are clean or unclean, he says: "in the waters, and in the seas, and in the torrents." But the Latin manuscripts have "in the sea", because it was too unusual to carry the plural number over from the Greek and to say not in mari but in maribus, chiefly on account of the ambiguity, lest not seas (maria) but mares, that is, males, should be understood. Yet it is no less unusual, though it has nevertheless been translated so, to say "from bloods" (de sanguinibus), since the Latin language does not admit the plural number of sanguis, not even in the nominative case itself. For although no one says maribus from mare, still maria is said, whereas sanguines is not said; and yet it is written: "Deliver me from bloods", and: "I will not gather their assemblies from bloods." Therefore maribus too could have been said in the same way, had it not been, as I said, to avoid ambiguity. In this place, however, Scripture has put "torrents" for "rivers", whereas torrents properly so called are winter streams, which dry up in summer and therefore cannot have fish. Hence some of our translators preferred to render it not "torrents" but "rivers". But that Scripture uses "torrents" for "rivers" is shown clearly enough by that passage of the Psalm where we read: "and you will give them drink from the torrent of your delight." For by the name of torrent it did not mean anything that flows for a time and then dries up, since it goes on to say: "for with you is the fountain of life", which is certainly eternal and unfailing.
"But these you shall eat of the creeping winged things that walk on four, which have legs above its feet." He did not say "above their own feet".
"And you shall be holy, since holy I." "Am" is understood; hence most of our translators rendered it: "since I am holy."

"And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying." This is a very common expression, extremely frequent in the Scriptures: "he spoke, saying". But the one that follows is found more rarely, and it puts the poverty of the Latin tongue under strain. For the Greek has: kai ereis pros autous legōn, which could be expressed in Latin as "and you shall say to them, saying"; but it is less jarring to say "and you shall tell them, saying", and this is closer to the Greek, because the Greek too did not say lexeis pros autous legōn, but ereis pros autous legōn.

"A woman, whoever conceives seed and bears a male, and she shall be unclean seven days." Most of our translators were unwilling to render this, but put it thus: "A woman, whoever conceives seed and bears a male, shall be unclean seven days." So this expression, since it is unusual in Greek speech as well, could have been left untranslated in Greek too; but since the Greeks did not mind translating it, why the Latins minded I do not know.

"Thirty-three days she shall sit in her clean blood." Likewise it was said of the woman who bore a female: "she shall sit in her clean blood", but with the same days doubled, that is, for sixty-six days. So "she shall sit" is said for "she shall remain"; for she was not forbidden to rise from her seat for so many days.
"If a man has on the skin of his body a shining scar of a mark." It is to be noted that Scripture uses "scar" not only for the mark of a wound but even for a mark of color alone.
"And there is in the skin of his color a touch of leprosy." By "touch" he means the spot itself, because the man himself has been touched by leprosy.
"And the priest shall see him and shall defile him"; in place of "shall pronounce him defiled".
"And the hair that is in the touch turns white"; that is: turns to white.
"And the priest shall cleanse him, for it is a mark": he shall pronounce him cleansed, just as "he shall defile", which he said above, means "he shall pronounce him defiled".

"And the priest sees him, and behold, the sign has changed in the skin, and the priest shall defile him." It has "and" in excess; for with that conjunction removed the sense is complete, in this way: "But if the sign has turned in the skin after the priest saw him to cleanse him, and he has been seen again by the priest, and the priest sees him, and behold, the sign has changed in the skin, the priest shall defile him."

"And if the touch of leprosy is in a man, he shall come to the priest; and the priest shall see, and behold, a white scar in the skin, and this has changed the hair white, and from the sound part of the living flesh in the scar"; that is: it has changed the hair to a white color in the scar; and it has changed it from the sound part of the living flesh, that is, because it does not have hair such as the sound part of the living flesh has.

Speaking of the leper, he says: "and unclean, unclean he shall be called", as though it were not enough to say once: "unclean he shall be called". Although a number of manuscripts have it so, in another Greek copy we found it said once: "unclean he shall be called". Likewise a little later he says: "since he is unclean, he shall be unclean", which could not be expressed in Latin from the Greek as it is put there. For the Greek says: akathartos ōn akathartos estai, as if to say "being existent unclean, he shall be unclean". But ōn, which the Greek used, is not the same as "existent" (existens); rather, it would be essens, if that could be said, from the verb "to be" (esse), not from the verb "to exist" (existere).
"And a garment, if there is in it a touch of leprosy." He could have said in the usual way: "and if there is a touch of leprosy in a garment".
"Or in any vessel of skin, in whichever there is in it a touch." It would have been enough to say: "in whichever there is a touch".

"And behold, the touch has not changed its appearance"; that is, the color in which it is seen. For it does not mean the sight by which it itself sees; for by "touch", indeed, he means the spot itself.
"And the priest, taking some of the measure of oil, shall pour it into the priest's left hand." He did not say "into his own left hand", although he certainly does pour it into his own.
"To a man, a man whoever has a discharge."
"And a man whoever, from him there goes out a lying of seed."
"And everything upon which he sleeps upon it."
"And everything upon which he sits upon it shall be unclean."

"And he shall send it away in the hand of a man made ready, into the wilderness"; that is: he shall send it away into the wilderness in the hand of a man made ready for this. He was speaking of the scapegoat when he said this. It is to be noted, however, how Scripture says "in the hand".
"A man, a man of the children of Israel"; that is: from among the children of Israel. This repetition seems to signify any man whatever, that is: this one or that one.
"The nakedness of your father and the nakedness of your mother you shall not uncover." By this expression he forbade intercourse with these persons.

"The nakedness of your father's brother you shall not uncover, and you shall not go in to his wife; for she is your kinswoman." He has put "and" for "that is"; for by "the nakedness of his father's brother", that is, the nakedness of his paternal uncle, he means the private parts of the uncle's wife.
"And the land loathed those who sit upon it"; that is: who have their seats there, which means "who dwell" there.

"And when you reap the harvest of your land, you shall not finish reaping your harvest of thy field." That he began with the plural and ended with the singular number, most Latin translators were unwilling to render, but said "of your field" where "of thy field" is said, as though a Greek could not say this. Rather, the expression ought to have been noted than corrected.

"Whoever takes his sister, of his father or of his mother, and sees her nakedness, and she sees his nakedness, it is a disgrace; they shall be destroyed in the sight of their race: he has uncovered the nakedness of his sister; they shall receive [their] sin." He has put "sin" for "the punishment of sin".

"And you shall separate yourselves between the clean animals and the unclean animals, and between the clean and unclean birds." He said, "you shall separate yourselves between the clean and the unclean", since the clean are separated from the unclean, or the unclean from the clean; it is an altogether new expression. For it is one thing to say "you shall separate between the clean animals and the unclean animals", as he very often speaks, and another what he has just said: "you shall separate yourselves", as though, in separating those things from one another, they would separate themselves from both, as if judging between the two.

"Speak to the priests, the sons of Aaron, and you shall say to them: In souls they shall not be defiled among their people, except for a relative who is nearest to them." He means in mourning, which is owed to the souls of the dead; for they are mourned because they have departed.
"And you shall not shave baldness for the dead, and upon their flesh they shall not cut cuttings." The usual expression would be "they shall not cut their flesh with cuttings".

"A harlot and a profane woman they shall not take, nor a woman cast out by her husband, since he is holy to the Lord his God." He did not say "since they are holy", but spoke as though of one, although he began with the plural. Then follows in the singular: "he shall sanctify him; he offers the gifts of the Lord your God; he is holy, since I, the Lord, am holy, who sanctify them"; again he has concluded with the plural.

"But if a priest acquires a soul bought with money, he shall eat of his bread." He did not say "she shall eat", although he said "soul", which is of the feminine gender; but he rather had in view what he meant to signify by "soul", that is, a person.
"And the daughter of a man who is a priest, if she is to a foreign man"; that is: if she marries a foreign man.

"And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: A calf or a sheep or a goat, when it is born, and it shall be seven days under its mother." It seems to have "and" in excess, in keeping with the very common expressions in the Scriptures which most Latin translators were unwilling to render.

"And I will be sanctified in the midst of the children of Israel"; which means "I will be held holy". For it is not that the Lord is not holy apart from the children of Israel as well. It is in this sense that it is also said in the Lord's Prayer: "Hallowed be your name", that is, may it be held holy by men.

"Speak to the children of Israel, and you shall say to them: The solemn feasts of the Lord, which you shall call called holy, these are my solemn feasts. Six days thou shalt do works." Although he said it was to be spoken to many, he afterwards speaks as though to one.

"And you shall count for yourselves from the morrow of the sabbath, on which he offered the sheaf of the offering laid upon the altar, seven full weeks thou shalt count." He did not say "you shall count", although above he was speaking to many.

"And when the son of the Israelite woman had named the name, he cursed." Although he did not add "of God" here, it is nevertheless clear that the name he cursed is to be understood as the name of God.

"A man, a man, if he curses his God, he shall receive sin." Here it appears plainly enough that it is a manner of speaking when "a man, a man" is said, as though to say "this man or that", that is, any man whatever; not, as some have thought, that "a man, a man" is said as a term of praise, as if to say "a man, but a man", that is, not just anyone, like a beast, but one who is truly a man. That this sense is not true, but that this is a manner of speaking in the Scriptures, is openly shown here, since it is said of one who is blamed, not of one who is praised.

When he was treating of the slaves whom the Israelites were permitted to have, he says: "and they shall be yours as a possession forever", although certainly neither masters nor slaves could be everlasting, since they die. So he said "forever" where no fixed limit of time is set for how long they are to serve, such as was set for those whom he commands to be released to their freedom in the remission.

"If you walk in my precepts and observe my commandments and do them, and I will give you rain in its season." The "and" is superfluous to the usage of our speech, but it is added after the manner of the Scriptures; for "I will give you" was what followed.

"And if even so you do not obey me, and I will add to chastise you sevenfold for your sins." Here too the "and" is superfluous; for "I will add to chastise you" was what followed. As for his saying "sevenfold", it is to be taken to stand for every number.
BOOK FOUR. EXPRESSIONS IN NUMBERS.
"And there shall be with you each one according to the tribe of each of the leaders."

"For the sons of Simeon, according to their kindreds, according to their peoples, according to the houses of their families, according to the number of their names, according to their head, all the males from twenty years old and upward, everyone who goes out in strength, their muster." This idiom, in which it does not say "the sons of Simeon" or "of the sons of Simeon" but "for the sons of Simeon" in the dative case, and keeps to it from here on for the other tribes, was not translated by the Latin translators we have been able to consult. In the tribe of Reuben alone, which was counted first, this idiom does not occur: there it does not say "For the sons of Reuben according to their kindreds," and so on, but "And the sons of Reuben, the firstborn of Israel, were according to their kindreds," and after that it goes on as with the others.
"And the sons of Israel did according to all that the Lord commanded Moses and Aaron; so they did."
"The priests who were anointed, whose hands of theirs they consecrated to serve as priests."
"And they shall put on it all its vessels with which they minister in them."

"And he shall make restitution to whom he sinned against, to him." Some, unwilling to translate this idiom, put the words into proper order and rendered: "And he shall make restitution to him against whom he sinned."

"Man or woman, whoever shall have done any of all human sins." It does not use the feminine "whoever" (quaecumque). This is an idiom in which the masculine gender has claimed the pronoun even though the feminine is placed after it, and this idiom is not customary.
"Of a man, of a man, if his wife has transgressed": the idiom is worth noting not only because it doubled the noun, saying "of a man, of a man," but also because it added "his."
"If a spirit of jealousy comes upon him, and she has not been defiled, and the man shall bring his wife to the priest": the "and" is superfluous, but this idiom is customary in the scriptures.

"It shall be the water of conviction which is cursed, this." The word order has made this idiom unusual. It could be said in the usual way thus: "This shall be the water of conviction which is cursed," or "It shall be this water of conviction which is cursed," or in whatever other way it can be said by arranging the words in the usual manner.

"Be innocent of the water of conviction which is cursed, this (haec)." In this idiom not only does the word order sound unusual, but the case has also been changed. The complete and usual form would be: "Be innocent of this (hac) water of conviction which is cursed," or "of the water of conviction, this (hac), which is cursed."

"And she shall be swollen the belly" (uentrem), instead of "swollen in the belly" (uentre). This idiom is frequent among Latin authors as well; but those of our translators who were unwilling to render it said: "and her belly shall swell."
"Man or woman, whoever (quicumque) has greatly vowed a vow": it did not say the feminine quaecumque.
"And he shall be shaved his head": this idiom is of the same kind as the one above, "she shall be swollen the belly."

"Six covered wagons and twelve oxen, a wagon from two leaders and a calf from each one." In this idiom I thought it worth noting that the same animals it had called oxen are called calves; but this too is said to be a Greek idiom.
"One leader daily, a leader daily they shall offer their gifts," instead of saying: "one leader on each day."
"One calf from the oxen and one he-goat from the goats."

"And there shall not be among the sons of Israel one of the sons of Israel approaching the holy things." It seems it would have been enough to say: "And there shall not be among the sons of Israel one approaching the holy things," or at any rate: "There shall not be one of the sons of Israel approaching the holy things."
"And Moses and Aaron and the whole congregation of the sons of Israel did to the Levites; according to what the Lord commanded Moses concerning the Levites, so the sons of Israel did to them."

"And a man, a man, whoever is clean and is not on a distant journey and has failed to keep the Passover, that soul shall be cut off from his people." So "a man, a man" is an idiom, as if it said: "whatever man, this one or that."

"And when the cloud had gone up from the tabernacle, and afterward the sons of Israel set out." It could have been complete as: "And when the cloud had gone up from the tabernacle, the sons of Israel set out."
"And they set out, the order of the camp of the sons of Judah, first."

"And the sons of Gershon and the sons of Merari will set out." It used a verb in the future tense although it is narrating a past event, just as earlier, when it spoke of the cloud at whose movement or halting the camp set out or stayed put. And from here on it uses this verb in the same way for the setting out of several groups.
"And Moses said to Hobab, son of Raguel the Midianite, the son-in-law of Moses." It does not say: "his son-in-law."
"And he said to him: I will not go, but to my own land and to my own kindred": "I will go" is understood.

"And the mixed crowd that was among them, they craved a craving." It put the singular for the plural, saying "mixed crowd" (promiscuus) rather than "mixed people" (promiscui); and yet it gave a plural verb when it said "they craved."

"But now our soul dry, nothing except on the manna our eyes." The words "is" and "are" are missing; the complete form would be: "our soul is dry, our eyes are on nothing except the manna." And in fact some translators rendered it this way and added words that are not in the Greek.
"And they ground it in a mill."
"Six hundred thousand foot soldiers among whom I am among them."

"And he took some of the spirit which upon him": "was" or "will be" is understood. This idiom, called ellipsis, is very common in Greek and, I think, in Hebrew as well, yet the Latin translators were reluctant to render it, although it is frequent in Latin too, if less so than in Greek.
"And the Lord struck the people a very great blow": the idiom to be noted was "struck a blow" (plagam), not "struck with a blow" (plaga), which is the usual form.
"And the man Moses very meek": "was" is understood.
"And the anger of the Lord's wrath upon them": "arose" is understood.
"And behold, Miriam leprous as snow": here too "became" is understood.
"And what is the land in which they dwell on it; and what are the cities in which they live in them."

"That very place which they named the Valley of the Cluster," after it had said earlier: "they came into the Valley of the Cluster." So this was said by anticipation: not that the place was already called this when they came, but that it was already called this when this book was written.
"Since he is more stronger than we": the idiom would be more usual if it did not have "more."
"And they brought out terror of the land which they had explored it."
"The land which we passed through it to explore is a land that devours those who dwell on it." The usual way to say it would have been: "the land which we passed through to explore."
"The land which we explored it is good, very, very."
"And the whole congregation said to stone them in stones." It does not say "with stones," although "to stone" alone could have sufficed in the usual idiom.
"And how long will they not believe me in all the signs with which I did among them?" It does not say: "which I did among them."
"But my servant Caleb, since another spirit in him and he has followed me, and I will bring him into the land": it would be usual if it did not have "and."
"And I will bring him into the land into which he entered there." In the usual idiom "into which he entered" would suffice.

"And the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying." This is put in even though the Lord was already speaking above. Scripture often does this: when it means to say something further, it introduces again as speaking someone who was already speaking.
"As many as murmured upon me." It does not say "about me" or "against me."

"And they shall possess as an inheritance the land which you departed from it." The usual form would be "from which you departed"; but here it says, in a novel way, "which you departed," and "from it" is added, as the scriptures tend to speak. It is like "and you approached the deep-resounding rocks" (accestis scopulos), that is, "you approached the rocks," where it does not say "to the rocks"; and "they came down the places" (deuenere locos), where it does not say "to the places." So too "which you departed," where it does not say "from which you departed."
"I the Lord have spoken: unless I do so to this wicked congregation." One must certainly ask what is meant by the Greek ἦ μήν; for our translators have nearly everywhere rendered it as "unless."
"Into the land into which I am bringing you there."

"But if one soul sins unintentionally, it shall offer a yearling she-goat for sin. And the priest shall entreat for the unwilling soul, the one that sinned unintentionally before the Lord, to entreat for him; and it shall be forgiven him." In this sentence two idioms were worth noting. First, it says "and the priest shall entreat" and afterward says "to entreat," for both could be put together thus: "he shall entreat to entreat." Second, beginning with the feminine gender it ended with the masculine: having said "if one soul sins," it concluded with "to entreat for him," where "for that man" is understood. And in what it added, "and it shall be forgiven him," this does not show in Latin, because the pronoun ei is of every gender; but in Greek the masculine is plain, since it has αὐτῷ where "him" (ei) is put here. As for the phrase "for the unwilling soul," this is understood as "which sinned unwillingly," not "which is unwilling to have an offering made for it." Indeed it explained this in what follows, when it said "the one that sinned unintentionally." And "unwilling" (inuita) was used because what is said in Greek, ἀκουσιασθείσης, could not be expressed in Latin; for one could not say "nolentata," or anything else derived from what someone has done unwillingly.
"And any soul that shall have done with a hand of pride": "sin" is understood. Note also that it says "with a hand of pride," putting "hand" for deed or power.
"Let the man die by death; stone him with stones, all the congregation." "Die by death," "stone with stones," and "stone (plural), all the congregation" are idioms unusual for us.
"And take, each one, his censer."
"And they went down, they and all that are theirs." It put the present for the past: "are" for "were" or "had been."
"And all Israel who round about them fled at their cry": "was" is understood, that is: all Israel which was round about them.

"Because they sanctified the censers of these sinners in their souls." It did not say: "because these sinners sanctified the censers in their souls"; but as if someone were asking whose censers they were, instead of saying "their own" it said "of these sinners." And it left us to understand who sanctified them, namely they themselves.
"And behold, the rod sprouted into the house of Levi": Latin usage would require "in the house of Levi."

"And I have taken your brothers the Levites from the midst of the sons of Israel, a giving given to the Lord." This idiom was translated into Latin this way out of necessity; for the Greek has δόμα δεδομένον. Anyone wishing to express this in Latin would have to say datum datum, because δόμα is also datum, "a thing given." So the apostle says: "Not that I seek the gift (datum), but I seek the fruit," where the Greek has δεδομένον; and in Genesis, "Abraham gave gifts (data) to his sons," the Greek has δόματα; and in the Gospel, "you know how to give good gifts (data) to your children," the Greek has δόματα. But δεδομένον, "given," is not a noun but a participle. So one could say datum datum, as if "a given thing that is given," were it not that the ambiguity had to be avoided. Some of our translators, trying to avoid this ambiguity, said donum datum, "a gift given"; but donum in Greek is δῶρον, not δόμα. So that would not be right in this passage, since God does not say that this was presented to him as a gift by the sons of Israel, but rendered in place of the firstborn who were owed to him. Hence both what is rendered and what is presented as a gift can be called "things given." And so every gift is also a thing given, but not every thing given is also a gift, because not everything that is given is thereby also bestowed as a gift.

"Every firstfruit of oil and every firstfruit of wine and of wheat, their firstfruit, whatever they give to the Lord, I have given them to you." It did not say: "every firstfruit offering I have given it to you"; but having said "every firstfruit" and listed what it consisted of, it went on: "I have given them (ea) to you." Nor did it even say "I have given it (eam) to you" or "them (eas)," meaning the firstfruits; instead it used the neuter gender, which is indeed commonly done in an absolute construction in Latin as well. Nor does the singular primitia, "firstfruit," seem to be Latin; for primitiae is normally used only in the plural. But if our translators could render what they found in Greek, "I will not gather their assemblies from bloods," and in another place, "The man of bloods and deceit the Lord will abhor," although sanguis, "blood," in Latin is only singular, why should they have been reluctant here too to express the singular primitia as the Greek has it? Some translators, however, put "firstfruits" in the plural and in the accusative case, saying: "All the firstfruits I will give to you." Thus they were unwilling to translate either idiom, both unusual for us, as they found them in the Greek.

"Speak to the sons of Israel, and let them take to you a red heifer," as if it said: "let them bring to you"; or at any rate both would be said in the usual way: "let them take and bring to you a red heifer."
"And he shall wash his body with water." This would be understood even if it did not have "with water."
"And he shall put it outside the camp into a clean place." It did not say "in a clean place," which is the Latin idiom.
"Every open vessel, whichever do not have a binding bound upon them."
"And Moses took the rod which before the Lord": "was" is understood.

"Because you did not believe, to sanctify me before the sons of Israel," that is, to declare my holiness. It is in line with this idiom that it was said: "And for them I sanctify myself," and in the Lord's Prayer: "Hallowed be your name."
"And we sojourned in Egypt many days," for "many years."

"And Edom said to him," that is, the nation itself (for Edom, who was Esau, was no longer living), just as those who sent the messengers were called Israel, which had earlier been the name of one man.

"And the sons of Israel say to him: We will pass by the mountain; but if we drink of your water, I and my cattle, I will give you payment." Quite elegantly it passes from the plural to the singular, as though Israel were speaking, after it had said "the sons of Israel" and had begun with plural verbs, namely "we will pass" and "we drink."

"And the whole congregation saw that Aaron had been released." This word, "released" in the sense of "dead," is not easily found in the scriptures. It occurs also in the Gospel, where Simeon says: "Now you release your servant in peace." Yet the Greek there has ἀπολύεις, which sounds as if it comes from "dissolving" rather than from "releasing"; for it did not say ἀφεῖς, which is undoubtedly "you release."

"And they wept for Aaron thirty days, all the house of Israel." It did not say "it wept," nor did it say "the whole" or "the entire," but "all," as if there were many; just as "every man" (omnis homo), said of all men, is of course quite different from "the whole man" (totus homo), said of one. But scripture constantly puts "all" for "whole."
"And the people spoke ill to God and against Moses." It did not say "of God" but "to God." Some, however, unwilling to translate this idiom, rendered it "they spoke ill of God."
"Pray therefore to the Lord that he take the serpent away from us": just as in Exodus "the frog" was said, singular for plural.

"And it came to pass, when the serpent bit a man, and he looked at the bronze serpent, and he was living." This idiom not only changes the form of the verb, ending with the imperfect after the perfect form of the past tense, but also has an extra "and."
"And setting out from Oboth they encamped at Achalgai, across in the wilderness," that is, in the farther wilderness.
"And he struck the donkey in the rod." It did not say "with the rod" but "in the rod."
"I called you to curse my enemies, and behold, you have blessed a blessing." It did not say "with a blessing," but spoke as if it said: "behold, you have spoken a blessing."
"Whatever things God puts into my mouth, this I will take care to speak." It did not say: "these things I will take care."
"Come with me further to another place from which you will not see him from there."

"And the Lord said to Moses: Take the leaders of the people and expose them to the Lord facing the sun, and the anger of the Lord's wrath will be turned away from Israel." Although it is the Lord speaking, he did not say: "and expose them to me, and my anger will be turned away from Israel."

"She is of a house of a family in Midian." He said this of the woman who was struck down together with the Israelite adulterer. By these words, as I think, he meant it to be understood that she was of noble birth, so that he called her "of a house of a family." In the same way, people now commonly say "father of a family" and "mother of a family" as a mark of wealth.

"And the Lord spoke to Moses and Eleazar the priest, saying: Take the beginning of the whole congregation of the sons of Israel from twenty years old and upward." Note what he called "the beginning": namely, the people in the strength of their age.
"That the sons of Israel may obey him," and "at his mouth they shall go out," and "at his mouth they shall come in," that is, when he commands.

"And Moses did according to what the Lord commanded him; and taking Joshua, he set him before Eleazar the priest," and so on. What was worth noting here is that, having already said "and Moses did according to what the Lord commanded him," it repeats the same thing.
"And he commissioned him according to what the Lord commanded Moses." It does not say "according to what the Lord commanded him."
"A tenth, a tenth of fine flour mixed with oil for one lamb"; that is, one tenth for each lamb. For by saying "a tenth, a tenth" it indicated that the tenths are to be repeated for each lamb.

"And in the first month, on the fourteenth of this month, a feast day; for seven days you shall eat unleavened bread." Note that the feast day is celebrated over several days and yet is called "feast day," not "feast days," meaning the celebration of the festival itself, however many days it lasts.

"And in the seventh month, on one of the month." It is in line with this idiom that Genesis says: "And there was evening and there was morning, one day"; for there, as here, the Greek has ἡμέρα μία. So those who translate here "on the first day of the month" have passed over a necessary idiom, although they have not departed from the meaning of the words.
"One calf from the oxen, one ram." It does not say "from the sheep," as it said "from the oxen," though that phrase too, if it were missing, the sense would be complete.
"Seven yearling lambs without blemish." The phrase "without blemish," which it attached to the lambs, is understood throughout, that is, of the calf and of the ram as well.
"A tenth, a tenth for one lamb, for the seven lambs," that is, one for each.

"Besides your vows, and your freewill offerings, and your whole burnt offerings, and your sacrifices, and your drink offerings, and your peace offerings." I would not note this idiom if it were even Greek. For it does not continue as it had begun, "besides your vows and your freewill offerings" and so on, all in the ablative (exceptis uotis uestris et uoluntariis uestris); nor does it say "besides your vows" in the accusative (excepta uota uestra), so as to begin with what is, so to speak, the solecism itself. Instead, having first said correctly, in the usual idiom, "besides your vows" (exceptis uotis uestris), it then attached the rest in another case, where the ablative exceptis cannot be understood, but only the accusative excepta. Neither Greek nor Latin idiom allows this.
"A man, a man, whoever vows a vow to the Lord," instead of "every man."

"But when a woman vows a vow to the Lord, or binds herself with a binding in her father's house in her youth." Here, in the manner of the scriptures, it calls a female a "woman" even if she is a virgin. Hence also the apostle says of Christ: "born of a woman."
"And her father hears her vows and her bindings with which she bound herself." "She bound bindings" is an idiom.
"She bound herself against her soul," that is, against the pleasures of her soul.
"And her father has kept silent, and all her vows shall stand." Here "and" is extra; for the complete sense is: "if her father hears and keeps silent, all her vows shall stand."
"But if she has been made a man's": "has married" is understood; this is how scripture speaks.
"And her vows upon her": "are" is understood, and some translators even added it.

"All things whatever that go out of her lips, according to her vows and according to her bindings which against her soul, does not remain for her," where the plural would be expected, so as to say "do not remain for her." Some did in fact translate it that way, avoiding what looked like a solecism.
"A thousand from a tribe and a thousand from a tribe, from all the tribes of Israel." Surely it did not say "a thousand" twelve times? And yet this repetition means a thousand from each.
"They killed in the sword," which would usually be said "they killed with the sword."
"And all their cities which in their dwelling places": "were" is understood.
"And they burned their villages in fire," which would usually be said "they burned with fire."
"And the whole multitude of women who have not known lying with a male, keep alive." Nowhere is it more clearly evident that in Hebrew idiom even virgins are commonly called women.
"And from half of them you shall take, and you shall give them to Eleazar the priest as the firstfruits of the Lord." For the second verb it did not use the plural "you shall give."

"And the souls of human beings, of the women who had not known lying with a man, all the souls, thirty-two thousand." Here too the earlier idiom is confirmed: those who have not known lying with a man, that is, virgins, are also called women.

"And Moses and Eleazar the priest took the gold from the commanders of thousands and from the centurions and brought them into the tabernacle of the testimony." It seems it ought to have said "and brought it into the tabernacle of the testimony," since it had already said that gold was received. Most Latin manuscripts do read that way. But the plural seems to have been used, so that it said "brought them," because many vessels had been listed above in which this gold consisted.
"And cattle, a multitude was to the sons of Reuben and the sons of Gad, a very great multitude." It did not say: "and there was a multitude of cattle."

"And they saw the region of Jazer and the region of Gilead, and it was a place, a place for cattle." The word "place," which it said twice, is not to be run together in reading aloud; there should be a slight pause: "and it was a place," and then should follow: "a place for cattle." For the repetition was introduced elegantly, as if one were waiting to hear what kind of place it was.

"And the sons of Reuben and the sons of Gad came and said to Moses and to Eleazar the priest and to the leaders of the congregation, saying." This expression, "they said, saying," is neither Greek nor Latin; it seems to be Hebrew.
"Let this land be given to your servants as a possession": they spoke as though of other people, when they were asking for it for themselves.

"For they did not follow after me, except Caleb the son of Jephunneh." It seems he ought to have said praeter Chaleb filium Iephone, in the accusative; but he put it in the nominative because "they followed" came before. This expression is found in Latin too, but it is rare.
"Until the whole generation, those doing evil in the sight of the Lord, was consumed." He did not say faciens maligna ("doing evil," in the singular), nor facientium maligna ("of those doing evil").
"And they approached him and said." He does not use the usual expression accesserunt ad eum ("they came up to him"), but accesserunt ei.
"And you shall build for yourselves cities for your baggage": as if he were saying, "You shall build cities for yourselves because of your baggage."

"Our baggage and our wives and all our cattle will be in the cities of Gilead; but your servants will all cross over armed." They did not say, "But we will all cross over armed," but spoke as though of other people.

"And Moses commended to them Eleazar the priest and Joshua [?] the son of Nun and the heads of the families of the tribes of Israel." He does not say, "Moses commended them to Eleazar the priest," which the order of ordinary usage would certainly have required. For it was by these men that they were brought into the land they were seeking. So it seems that the people were commended to those by whom they were being brought into the land they had asked for, rather than that those who were bringing them in were commended to those whom they were bringing in.
"But if they do not cross over armed with you to war before the Lord, and transfer their baggage." There is an extra "and."
"And Moses gave them, the sons of Gad and the sons of Reuben." There is an extra "them."
"And there was no water there for the people to drink." Here "to drink" (bibere) stands for "for drinking" (ad bibendum).
"Speak to the sons of Israel, and you shall say to them." "Speak to the sons of Israel" would seem to be enough.
"And all their molten idols, you shall destroy them." There is an extra "them."
"This shall be for you the boundaries of the sea." He did not say, "These shall be for you."
"And this shall be for you the boundaries toward the north": the same expression is repeated.
"And the cities shall be theirs to dwell," instead of the usual phrase, "for dwelling."
"They shall be refuges for you, for the manslayer to flee there": in ordinary usage one could say, "so that the manslayer may flee there."

"And for the sojourner who among you, these cities as a refuge." "Sojourner" (incolae) is put in the singular; that is, "for this sojourner who among you," because "is" is missing. For he does not say "who is among you," the very familiar expression, but uses one that is rarer in Latin than in Greek.
BOOK FIVE. EXPRESSIONS IN DEUTERONOMY.
As far as the great river, the river Euphrates. It did not say: as far as the great river Euphrates.
And the judgment that is too hard from you, you shall bring it to me. It did not say “too hard for you” but “from you”, that is, so hard that it cannot be judged by you.

If any of these men shall see this excellent land which I swore to their fathers, except Caleb, son of Jephunneh; he shall see it. We noted this expression in the book of Numbers as well: it did not say “except Caleb, son” in the accusative (filium), but in the nominative (filius).
For the Lord your God has blessed thee in every work of thy hands. It does not say: has blessed you in every work of your hands, although it had just said “your” in the plural, not “thy”.

Now therefore arise, set out, and pass over the valley of Arnon; behold, I have delivered into thy hands Sihon king of Heshbon. It did not say “into your hands”, but passed from the plural to the singular.

For what great nation is there that has it a god drawing near to them? Two things are to be noted here: first, that it says “that has it”; second, that it does not say “drawing near to it” but “drawing near to them”.
And you saw no likeness, but a voice — although a voice cannot be seen. But he used this verb in a general way, as though seeing applied to every bodily sense.
Into which you are entering there to inherit it: the sense would be complete even if “there” had not been added.

And he brought you out of the iron furnace, out of Egypt: by “iron furnace” he meant harsh tribulation to be understood. In the same sense it is said of Joseph in the Psalms: The iron passed through his soul.
And I shall not cross this Jordan — as though there were another Jordan as well. From this expression, I think, people often also say “this world”, as though there were no other.
But if you beget sons and sons of your sons: the expression is to be noted, in which grandfathers too are said to beget grandsons.

And there you will seek the Lord your God, and you will find him when you seek him out with all thy heart and with all thy soul in thy tribulation: it did not say “with all your heart and with all your soul in your tribulation”.

Ask the former days which were before thee: it is to be understood as days, not men. Likewise this too is to be noted, as also above: although it said “ask” in the plural, it added “before thee” in the singular, not “before you”.

Or whether God has tried to go and take for himself a nation from the midst of a nation: “tried” is put for “willed”. Or does it mean something else? As for its saying “from the midst of a nation”, this is to be understood as “from the midst of nations”, the singular being put for the plural, just as we read “the serpent, the frog and the locust” written for serpents, frogs and locusts.
According to all that the Lord your God did in Egypt before you as you looked on: nothing would be lacking even if “as you looked on” were not added.

And I stood between the Lord and you at that time to announce to you the words of the Lord, because you were afraid at the face of the fire and did not go up the mountain, saying: I am the Lord your God, and so on: he put “saying” for “when he said”.
And the stranger who dwells in you: this is to be taken as said to the people, not as to a single man, since it is among a people that a stranger dwells.

For this reason the Lord your God has ordained for you that you should keep the sabbath day and to sanctify it. If it did not have “and”, the expression would not seem unusual: “that you should keep the sabbath day to sanctify it”; or certainly if it ran thus: “that you should keep the sabbath day and sanctify it”, or thus: “for this reason the Lord your God has ordained for you to keep the sabbath day and to sanctify it”. As it is, however, “that you should keep the sabbath day and to sanctify it” is an unusual expression, worth noting.

Take heed to yourself lest your heart be enlarged and you forget the Lord your God: it should be noted that enlargement of heart can also be spoken of in a bad sense. For exultation is understood by enlargement, and its opposite is constriction, that is, sadness. But both can be meant in either a good or a bad sense.
And it shall be, when your son asks you tomorrow, saying: he put “tomorrow” for any future time whatever.
Seven nations, great and many: how then many, if seven? But he called them many in the sense of having a great multitude.
You shall not make a covenant with them — he was speaking of the nations. So he used “covenant” for “pact”.

And you shall not take his daughter for your son; for she will make your son turn away from me, and he will serve other gods, and the Lord will be angry with indignation against you: it does not say “I will be angry”, but speaks as if of another.
Cities great and walled up to heaven: said hyperbolically.

Do not say in your heart, when the Lord your God has destroyed these nations before your face, saying: Because of my righteousness the Lord brought me in to inherit this good land. The order is: do not say in your heart, saying.
Lest those who inhabit the land from which you brought us out from there should say: “from there” is added according to the custom of Scripture.

What he did the might of the Egyptians. Some Latin translators, understanding this poorly, would not say “the might” but “to the might” or “to the army”, since some took what the Greek says, δύναμιν, to mean an army. But it is an elegant expression: “what he did their might” is to be understood as what he made of it, since he reduced it to nothing. But because it is said in the plural, it is somewhat obscure.

Whom the earth, opening its mouth, swallowed them up, and their houses and their tents. Two expressions are to be noted here: first, that “them” was added, when the “whom” said before could have sufficed; and second, that having said “their houses”, it added “and their tents”, as if in the desert they had any houses other than tents. But clearly he meant “houses” to be understood as the people belonging to them, as is said to the people itself: And now you, house of Jacob. Nor is this expression foreign to the Latin language, for the Romans too were called the house of Assaracus, because they traced their origin to the Trojan Assaracus.

For your eyes saw all the great works of the Lord which he did among you today. Although he was speaking of the works done in the desert during the time when they were led about there for forty years, he nevertheless said “today”, by which he meant this period, however many years that same period might have contained.

The land which the Lord swore to your fathers to give to them and to their seed after them. As if he said: that is, to their seed after them. For he did not give it to them as well; rather, he gave it to them in this sense, that he gave it to their seed.
But if with hearing you hear all his commandments which I command thee today: “with hearing” seems superfluous, but it is an expression most familiar to Holy Scripture.

And he will give rain to your land in its season, the morning rain and the late rain. Since “morning time” refers to the day, did he perhaps mean the first season of the year to be understood here? “Serotinus” (late), on the other hand, is not good Latin. But what they call ὄψιμον could not be rendered more properly from the Greek. Still, “serotinus” is in common use in Latin too, but of something that has happened later than it should. Here, however, he meant rather the season of the year to be understood.

And when you have eaten and been satisfied, take heed to thyself lest thy heart be enlarged, and you transgress and serve other gods. We have already noted such expressions above: both the passing from singular to plural, and that by “be enlarged” he meant something bad to be understood, signifying harmful prosperity.
And the great river, the river Euphrates: such repetitions are customary in the Scriptures and set off the thing fittingly.

The Lord your God will lay your fear and your trembling upon the face of the whole earth: not the fear and trembling with which they themselves fear and tremble, but that by which they are feared and make others tremble.
You cannot eat in your cities the tithe of your grain: this stands for “you must not”.
And you shall burn the city in fire: we would more usually say “with fire”.
But if the way is far off from you — as if to say: the way will be long. He put an adverb in place of a noun.

And you shall lend at interest to many nations. Scripture calls money given as a loan “lending at interest” even if no interest is received; hence also that line in the psalm: Blessed is the man who shows mercy and lends. For our translators preferred to render it so, thinking that the sense rather than the words should be followed; for the Greek has δανείζει, that is, “lends at interest”.

And you shall rule over many nations, but over thee (tui) they shall not rule. As if to say: they, that is, the nations, shall not have dominion over you. For “tui” here is the genitive singular of this pronoun — whose dative is “tibi” — not the nominative plural, whose genitive is “tuorum”.
But if there is a needy man in thee among thy brothers. This is said not to one man but to the people; hence “in thee”.

But if there is a needy man in you among your brothers in one of your cities in the land which the Lord your God gives you, you shall not turn away your heart nor close your hand against your needy brother; opening you shall open your hands to him, a loan you shall lend him, as much as he asks and as much as he needs. Here certainly, since he is enjoining works of mercy, the cruelty of usury is by no means to be adopted. Hence it is clear that by “a loan you shall lend him” he meant that what the man asked was to be given as a loan. And the phrase “opening you shall open your hands” is of the same kind as what follows, “a loan you shall lend”: an expression customary in the holy Scriptures.

Having given a command about piercing the ear of a slave, he says: and you shall do likewise your maidservant, putting the accusative for the dative. He does not say “you shall do to your maidservant”, as the usage of our speech required.

But if there is a defect in it, lame or blind, or any evil defect. It does not say “lameness or blindness” — for these are the defects — but “lame or blind”, which are not defects but animals that have defects. This too is to be noted, that it says “evil defect”, as though there could be a good defect.
And none of the flesh which you sacrifice in the evening on the first day shall sleep until morning. “Shall not sleep” is said for “shall not remain that night”.

You shall not offer to the Lord your God a calf or a sheep in which there is in it a defect. The customary expression would be “in which there is a defect”; but this one is more customary in the Scriptures.
And you shall stone them in stones, and they shall die: in our usage one would say “with stones”, not “in stones”.
He shall not multiply horse for himself. He put “horse” for horses or cavalry; hence some have translated “cavalry”.
You cannot set over you a foreign man, because he is not your brother. “You cannot” is said for “you must not”.

According to all that thou didst ask of the Lord thy God at Horeb on the day of the assembly, saying. Although it said above “thou didst ask”, it added “saying” in the plural (dicentes), not in the singular (dicens).
For the Lord your God, who goes before with you: it did not say “goes before you”.
If you run into a bird's nest before your face on the road. Note that it says “run into” even with reference to something that is not moving.

But if you build a new house, you shall make a parapet for your roof, and you shall not commit homicide in your house, if he who fell should fall from it, that is: if he who fell should fall from the roof. A very unusual expression.

And having gone away she has been another man's, and the last husband hates her. Note that of two the latter is called “the last”. There is a similar expression in the Gospel too, when it is asked which of two brothers did the father's will and the answer is “the last”, though there were only two.

You shall not take a mill or the upper millstone in pledge, because this man takes a soul in pledge — meaning: because you take a soul in pledge if you do this. Next, it should be noted that he said “soul” for the life that the soul has in the body. From this expression comes also the line in the Gospel: Is not the soul more than food?

But if a man is caught stealing a soul from among his brothers, the sons of Israel: he put “soul” for “man”. Then it continues: and overpowering him has sold him — no less noteworthy an expression. For he chose not to say “it” (in the feminine), which would have been more consistent, since he had said “soul”, but “him”, that is, the man whom he had meant by “soul”.
If there is a debt in your neighbor, any debt whatever: the repetition of the word makes the expression noteworthy.

But if the man does not wish to take his brother's wife, then the woman shall go up to the gate, to the elders, and say: My husband's brother does not wish to raise up his brother's name in Israel; my husband's brother would not. Although Scripture loves repetitions of words, this repetition is nevertheless rather unusual; but it displays the emotion of the complaint all the more elegantly.
Cursed is everyone who sleeps with every beast: this stands for “lies with”. Then “with every beast” stands for “with any beast whatever”.

And you shall serve your enemies, whom the Lord your God will send against you. The Greek has λατρεύσεις where the Latin translated “you shall serve”. Scripture usually uses this verb for the service that is owed to God; hence those who render that service to idols are called idolaters. So here this verb is used in an unusual way. Yet it may also have this sense: that he has said so many grievous things, that they will be forced to serve their exceedingly arrogant enemies as if they were gods.

A nation whose voice of it you will not hear. This too is to be noted: that it says both “whose” and “of it”, as the Scriptures commonly speak; and that “whose voice you will not hear” stands for “whose language you will not understand”.

The man among you who is soft and very delicate will bewitch with his eye his brother and the wife who is in his bosom and the remaining children who are left to him, so as to give one of them some of the flesh of his children, whichever he eats, because nothing has been left to him in the distress and tribulation with which your enemies will afflict you in all your cities. It is to be noted how “he will bewitch him” is said here for “he will begrudge him”, as one left alive only to make it necessary to give him some of the flesh of the children, which necessity forces parents to take as food. For in Proverbs too, where the Latin manuscripts have “Do not dine with an envious man”, the Greek has ἀνδρὶ βασκάνῳ, and βάσκανος means one who bewitches.

And it shall be that, as the Lord rejoiced over you to do good to you. The Greek has “to do good you”, and this does not seem to be even a Greek idiom. Yet the accusative is understood to be put for the dative; hence the Latin translators preferred to say “to you” rather than “you”.

You have seen all that the Lord your God did in the land of Egypt before you to Pharaoh and all his servants and all his land, the great trials which thy eyes saw: note that those plagues are also called trials.

If your dispersion is from the uttermost part of heaven to the uttermost part of heaven, from there the Lord your God will gather you. It would be surprising if by “from the uttermost part of heaven to the uttermost part of heaven” it did not mean what it also often says, “from the uttermost part of the earth to the uttermost part of the earth”: perhaps because, inasmuch as this air of ours is also called heaven, it is joined to the earth.

It is not in heaven, saying: Who will go up into heaven and get it for us, and hearing it we will do it? Nor is it beyond the sea, saying: Who will cross the sea for us and get it for us, and hearing it we will do it? He put “saying” for “that you should say”: a novel expression.
And the Lord who accompanies to you with you.
And the Lord said to Moses: Behold, you will sleep with your fathers: by this word he signified his death.
You were embittering the things toward God: that is, you were embittering the things that are God's.
For I know that after my death you will do iniquity with iniquity: in Greek, however, “you will do iniquity” is said in one word, namely ἀνομήσετε.
And evils will meet you the last of days: for this is what the Greek has, for “in the last days” or “in the last of days”.

Is not this very one your father, who possessed you and made you and created you? The order is to be noted; for it seems he ought first to have said “created you and made you” and then “possessed you”. For how can one who does not exist be understood to be possessed?

With the fat of the kidneys of wheat. This metaphor is very unusual: the kidneys of wheat are to be understood as the inner parts of the wheat, from which flour is extracted; and this he also called fat. For the Greeks are accustomed to call flour too by this name; this is what the Greek has in Exodus, where it is written: carrying the flour on their shoulders. The Greek translator in fact put στέατα, which means fats.
Sons in whom there is no faith in them: an expression customary in the Scriptures.

For the Lord will judge his people and will be comforted in his servants: this stands for “will comfort his servants”; unless perhaps it says that he himself is comforted, by a transferred use of the word, as if from the indignation and offense with which the wicked offend him. But his comfort is to be understood in this way, not after the manner of men, just as with his anger, his jealousy and the like.
Where are their gods, in whom they trusted in them: the sense would be complete even without “in them”.
And I will swear my right hand: that is, “by my right hand”.

Rejoice, O heavens, together with him, and let all the angels of God worship him. Other manuscripts have: and let all the sons of God worship him. But it is not easy to find in the holy Scriptures that those who are angels in heaven are called sons of God.
BOOK SIX. EXPRESSIONS IN JOSHUA SON OF NUN.
"But you shall cross over armed, ahead of your brothers, every strong one": that is, every one among you who is strong.
"That you may know the way by which you shall go it": the sense would be complete even without "it."

"And it came to pass, when Joshua was in Jericho." This expression should be noted. They were not yet in that city, whose gates had been shut against them. So it was that they could not enter it until its walls had fallen, once the ark of the Lord had been carried around them. Therefore "in Jericho" means: in the land that belonged to Jericho.

It was said of Jericho, when it was shut up: "and no one came out of it, nor went in." Clearly "into it" is understood, not "out of it." In Greek this is called [?] kat' elleipsin, that is, by omission.

The Lord says to Joshua: "Behold, I deliver to you Jericho subdued, and its king who is in it, mighty in strength." It is remarkable that here he did not put the copulative conjunction, so as to say "and mighty in strength." Scripture uses that conjunction so constantly that it is found even where it gets in the way of the sense of an ordinary expression. Or are both Jericho and its king being called "mighty in strength"?

"And Joshua kept alive Rahab the harlot and her father's house, and she has dwelt in Israel to this day." We should note how Scripture says "to this day," which it says constantly. It was also said of those twelve stones, set up where the lower part of the Jordan had flowed away and the upper part had stood still while the ark, or the people, crossed over, that they were there "to this day." This seems to suggest that these things were narrated long after the events, and that these books were not written at the time when the events were very recent. But whoever thinks this, what will he say about this harlot? She certainly lived no longer than the span of one human life, and yet it is said "to this day." So this is said of things that were not established in such a way that those who established them would later change them. In the same way someone is said to be sent into perpetual exile because he is not punished with this penalty for a fixed period of time, not because anyone can be in exile perpetually, since a man himself cannot be perpetual. So too this harlot was not ordered to dwell in Israel for a limited time, and that is why it is said: "to this day."

The Lord says to Joshua: "The people have sinned and have transgressed my covenant, which I laid down for them." We should note how he calls "covenant" what he had commanded: that Jericho should be under the ban and that no one should take anything from it for himself.

The Lord, speaking to Joshua, says among other things: "Behold, I have given into your hands the king of Ai and his land. And you shall do to Ai as you did to Jericho and to its king, and you shall take the cattle as plunder for yourself." This expression deserves special notice. It is not only that he said "you shall take as plunder for yourself," as though the plunder were to belong to one man when it was to belong to all. Such expressions are very common, since God often speaks as if to one person when he is speaking to the people. What is new here is that Scripture said beforehand, "And the Lord said to Joshua," who was clearly one man. Yet when he said "you shall take as plunder for yourself," this was certainly not meant as a command that the plunder should belong to this one man, but to the whole people.

"And there was an ambush against the city from the sea." Someone who does not know would think this was a city on the coast. But it is the custom of the Scriptures to call the western side "from the sea" or "toward the sea," because on that side the land where these things took place is closer to the sea than on any other side.

"Stretch out your hand with the gaeson that is in your hand against the city." This expression would not need noting except for the word, which is obscure to those who do not use it. What a gaeson is cannot easily be understood. The translator Symmachus is said to have called it a shield. But the Septuagint translators, whom we follow in this discussion, put gaeson, and I wonder whether even in Greek they meant it to be understood as a Gallic spear or lance. For those weapons are called gaesa, and Virgil mentions them where he speaks of the Gauls pictured on the shield of Aeneas: "each brandishes two Alpine javelins in his hand."

"And they were in the midst of the camp, these on this side and those on that side." Two things should be noted in this expression. First, the enemies who were being defeated were in the middle, yet the words "these on this side and those on that side" are said as if of them, when it was rather the Israelites who were placed this way, having put the enemy in the middle to strike them down. Second, Scripture says they were "in the midst of the camp," calling "camp" even the battle lines drawn up for combat, although "camp" is not usually said except where an army halts to stay. Unless perhaps it is called a camp because they went with all their belongings.

"Except for the cattle and the spoils that were in the city, the children of Israel took plunder according to the command of the Lord, as the Lord had instructed Joshua."
