It is put this way, "except for the cattle and the spoils they took plunder," as if they had not taken these as plunder, when in fact these are precisely what they took as plunder. They are called "excepted" because these alone were not destroyed in that battle.

The Israelites answered the Gibeonites and said: "See that you are not dwelling in me; and how shall I make a covenant with you?" We have already noted such expressions above. "See that you are not dwelling in me" means "with me," that is, in the land God had promised them. Here too they seem to speak as if to one man, though more than one envoy had come to them. But, as is their manner, when they give an answer to a nation and a people they speak in the singular, just as God or their leader often does when speaking to them. We should also note that Scripture calls a pact of peace a covenant, as is its custom, for it often speaks this way.
"And it was reported to Joshua, saying: 'The five kings have been found hidden in a cave'": instead of "they reported, saying."
"So the Lord will do to all your enemies, whom you will defeat them": the sentence would lack nothing even without "them."

"And he took them all in war, because it came from the Lord that their hearts were strengthened to go out to battle against Israel, so that they might be destroyed." We should note that "the heart being strengthened" is not always to be taken in a good sense.
"You know the word that the Lord spoke to Moses, the man of God, concerning me and you": he did not say "his man."

"And the children of Joseph said: 'The hill country is not enough for us, and the Canaanite who lives in Beth-shan has chosen horse and iron.'" He said "chosen horse" instead of "chosen horses," which is not usual in our language. That is why some Latin translators did not want to translate it as "horse" but as "cavalry." But "chosen horse" is said for "horses" in the way that we commonly say "the soldier" for "soldiers."

"And their outlets were the Jordan, and the borders will turn back to the sea." He did not say "turned back," or at least "turn back," as is usually said of borders, but "will turn back," as though it were still to come, although this is a narrative of past events. In almost all these divisions of the land, tribe by tribe, Scripture speaks this way, using verbs in the future tense.

"That he who has struck a soul unwillingly may flee there." Here we should understand "soul" either as a man or as the life of the flesh, which comes about through the soul. It was with this expression that Joseph's brothers said: "Let us not strike his soul," that is, let us not kill him. For if the soul could be struck by a killer, the Lord would not say: "Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul."

"The Lord commanded by the hand of Moses." This is a very common expression in the Scriptures. In the same way it is said: "the word that came by the hand of this or that prophet," that is, given into his power to speak.
"And Joshua took knives of flint, in which he had circumcised the children of Israel." He did not say "with which he had circumcised," but "in which."

"And when Joshua sent them away to their homes, and he blessed them, saying." The copulative conjunction, that is "and," seems superfluous here, for it could be said: "And when Joshua sent them away to their homes, he blessed them, saying."

Another expression should be noted as well. Scripture said, "And Joshua blessed them, saying," and with these words made us eager to hear what Joshua said in blessing them. Yet all it added was: "They went away to their homes with great riches; and they divided with their brothers the plunder of their enemies, a great many cattle, silver and gold, and a great deal of clothing." This clearly belongs to the narrator rather than to the one giving the blessing.
"And they built an altar there by the Jordan, an altar great to see": this expression is familiar in Latin as well.
"And the children of Israel heard, and of those saying." He does not say "from those saying" or "saying."

"To serve the service of the Lord." Two things should be noted in this expression: "to serve the service," which is also found as a Latin expression, and "the service of the Lord," that is, the service owed or rendered to the Lord.

"And Phinehas the priest and all the leaders of the congregation who were with him, hearing the words that the sons of Reuben and the sons of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh had spoken, and they pleased them." "Hearing" is put for "they heard," or else "and" is superfluous here; for the sense is complete as: "hearing these words, they pleased them." Even so, it is not without inconsistency, since it should have said "when they had heard."

"And Joshua was elderly, advanced in days." We noted, when this was said of Abraham, that in the Scriptures "elderly" describes not only someone who has not yet reached old age, but also someone very old. Hence not everyone who is elderly is an old man, but every old man can be called elderly.
"And he brought the sea upon them and covered over them": he does not say "covered them," although some translators preferred to say that.
"Among all the nations which we passed through them": such expressions are common in the Scriptures, and they need not be noted as often as they occur.
BOOK SEVEN. EXPRESSIONS IN JUDGES.
And it came to pass, after Joshua had died, that the children of Israel inquired in the Lord (in domino). He did not say "inquired of the Lord" (dominum), as the usage of our language required.
And we shall make war in the Canaanite. He did not say "against the Canaanite" (adversus Chananaeum or contra Chananaeum), or at least "upon the Canaanite" (in Chananaeum).

And Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of the Lord, died, a son of a hundred and ten years. This repetition is unusual: having said "son of Nun", he repeated "son" and then added "of a hundred and ten years", so that he said "a son of a hundred and ten years" rather than "a man of a hundred and ten years". Yet it is found elsewhere too.
And all the generation were gathered to their fathers. The expression is worth noting: he did not say "was gathered" (apposita est), because they were many.
He delivered them in the hand of plunderers. He did not say "into the hand" (in manum), which Latin idiom seems to require.

And when the Lord raised up judges for them, and the Lord was with the judge. In the usual manner there is an extra "and" here, for the sentence would be complete as: "And when the Lord raised up judges for them, the Lord was with the judge." This too should be noted: passing from plural to singular, he did not say "with the judges" but "with the judge", that is, with each judge.

And it came to pass, when the judge died, and they turned back and again acted corruptly above their fathers. According to the usage of our language, the correct expression could have been: "And it used to happen, when the judge died, and they turned back and again acted corruptly above their fathers." If it did not have "and", it would be complete: "When the judge died, they turned back and again acted corruptly above their fathers", that is, more than their fathers.
Because this nation has forsaken my covenant so greatly. He said tanta for tantum, that is, "so much": a noun for an adverb, which is also found in Latin expressions, especially poetic ones.
And they did not hearken to my voice (vocis meae). This is rather a Greek expression.

The Spirit of the Lord was made upon him. The Spirit of the Lord was certainly not made, but was "made upon him". So it is said as if it were said: "it came about that he was upon him." By the same expression we also read in the Gospel: "he was made before me", that is, it came about that he was before me, which could otherwise be put as "he has been preferred to me".
And Ehud took the sword from upon his right thigh. Thus he could render what the Greek has, epanōthen [?]; for the expression is hardly Latin.

Now Eglon was a very slight man. This is said κατ' ἀντίφρασιν, that is, by an expression meaning the opposite, as what follows shows. For when he was struck, it is said that the fat closed over the wound, because the sword was not drawn out of his belly.
And he struck the foreigners into six hundred men (in sescentos viros). He did not say "six hundred men of the foreigners", or at any rate "the foreigners in six hundred men" (in sescentis viris).

Has not the Lord God of Israel commanded you: and you will go to Mount Tabor? He did not say "that you go", which would seem to follow. Instead he used an unusual expression, "Has he not commanded you: and you will go", so that we supply the verb placed above and it becomes "will you not go?" Or else, in the usual manner, it has an extra "and"; for if that conjunction is removed the sense runs smoothly: "Has not the Lord God of Israel commanded you: you will go to Mount Tabor and take with you ten thousand men?" and so on.
For I do not know the day on which the Lord prospers the angel with me. Does he prosper the doings of his angel who is with me, or does he make things prosper for me through the angel?

All his chariots, nine hundred chariots of iron. Wherever the pause is placed, the repetition is elegant. Either "all his chariots" comes first, followed by "nine hundred chariots of iron", or "all his nine hundred chariots" comes first, with "chariots of iron" added afterwards.
And the Lord terrified Sisera and all his chariots and all his camp with the edge of the sword before Barak. How did he terrify chariots, unless you understand those who were in the chariots?

And the Lord terrified Sisera and all his chariots and all his camp with the edge of the sword before Barak. "He terrified with the edge of the sword" is as if he said "he killed with the edge of the sword". So he terrified them when they were cut down by the sword.
And Sisera came down from upon his chariot. In this way it could be said in Latin what in Greek is ἀπάνωθεν.
And she covered him in her skin. He did not say "with her skin" (pelle) or "from her skin" (de pelle); for the Greek has ἐν τῇ δέρρει.

And it will be, if anyone comes to you and says, "Is there a man here?", and you will say, "There is not." With the conjunction removed it gives a consistent sense: "If anyone comes to you and says, 'Is there a man here?', you will say, 'There is not.'"
And the hand of the children of Israel went on, going. This is a customary and frequent expression.
And it was hardened against Jabin king of Canaan. The verb "was hardened" is used here in a new way, meaning "it was becoming strong and very powerful".
She pierced his head and struck. That is, she struck his head and pierced it.
So may all your enemies perish, O Lord; and those who love him are like the rising of the sun in its might. He did not say "those who love you", though he certainly wanted it understood of the Lord.
And it came to pass, when the man of Israel had sown. This does not signify one man but the nation itself.
Midian and Amalek and the children of the east went up, and they went up against him. This repetition of the verb does not seem to have the usual elegance or emotional force.
And I delivered you from the hand of Egypt. By "hand" he means power, and by "Egypt" the Egyptians.
And Gideon said to him, "Upon me, my lord." The word "attend" is understood, that is, "attend upon me". This expression is very familiar in the Scriptures.

And if the Lord is with us, and why have all these evils found us? It has an extra conjunction "and", as Scripture usually speaks. If it is removed, the sentence is complete: "And if the Lord is with us, why have all these evils found us?" The earlier conjunction could also be removed without harm to the sentence. Then, after he had said "Upon me, my lord", there would follow: "If the Lord is with us, why have all these evils found us?" This is what the usage of our own speech requires.

And a calf of seven years. Here it is plain how Scripture uses the word "calves", for according to the usage of our language an ox of seven years is certainly not a calf. In keeping with this expression, it is said of Shamgar that he killed six hundred men besides the calves of oxen, that is, besides the oxen.
And he sounded on the horn (cornea). "Trumpet" is understood, for the Greek does not have "trumpet" but only "horn".

Their camels were without number, but were like the sand that is at the lip of the sea. Plainly this is said hyperbolically (ὑπερβολικῶς) of their great number. This figure, in which "lip of the sea" stands for "shore", is constant in the Scriptures but rare in Latin manuscripts. Most translators wrote "shore", wishing to give the meaning of "lip" rather than the word "lip" itself. Yet if the Seventy translators had wanted to say "shore", the Greek language would not have lacked a word for it.
And he divided the three hundred men into three heads (principia). He put "heads" for "parts".
And the man of Ephraim said to Gideon. That is, the men of the tribe of Ephraim.
What is this word that you have done to us, that you did not call us when you went out to fight against Midian? He put "word" for "deed".
And they gave him seventy of silver. "Pounds" or something similar is understood. The translation from the Hebrew has "seventy pounds".
And in them Abimelech hired men. He said "in them" for "out of them", that is, with the seventy pounds of silver he hired men.
Empty and unruly men. He put "empty" for "light", whose opposite is "weighty". Hence it is said: "In a weighty people I will praise you."

And he went into his father's house at Ephrathah and killed his brothers, the sons of Jerubbaal, seventy men, upon one stone. He had already said above that the sons of Jerubbaal, that is, of Gideon, were seventy, and now he says that seventy were killed. Yet two fewer were killed: the one who did the killing and Jotham, the youngest, who hid. Of Jotham he adds: "And Jotham the youngest son of Jerubbaal was left, because he hid himself." So he gave the whole number for almost the whole.
And the men of Shechem despised in the house of Abimelech. He did not say "despised the house of Abimelech".
And they lay in wait against Shechem in four heads (principia). That is, in four parts. We have already noted this expression above.
And he took the people and divided them into three heads. He said "took" of the people who were with him. Here too he put "three heads" for "three parts".
And they went away, a man to his place. That is, each one.

And you will be to us for a head over all who live in Gilead. He did not say "you will be our head", for Scripture usually speaks this way. Hence the verse: "Be to me for a protecting God and for a house of refuge", and many others of this kind.
And she was his only one, and he had no son or daughter besides her. This is what had been said in "his only one"; but the thought is repeated to express emotion.
And he has no son or daughter besides her. "He has not" is said for "he had not", since past events are being narrated.
And his wife was barren and did not bear, though the word "barren" alone could have been enough.
And Manoah prayed to the Lord and said, "Upon me, O Lord: let the man of God whom you sent come to us again now." "Upon me" is said in such a way that "attend" is understood.

And he struck them leg upon thigh. This expression is unusual, yet it is an idiom and does not refer to some place on the body where a wound was given, as I explained in the Questions. It means that he struck them to the point of amazement and stupefaction.
And the man of Judah said, "Why have you come up against us?" He put the singular for the plural, for it was the men of Judah who said this, not one man.
Lest perhaps you fall upon me. This stands for "kill me". This expression too is explained in the Questions.

And they brought him up from the rock, and he came as far as the Jawbone. The place was given this name afterwards, from what Samson himself did there when, fighting with a donkey's jawbone, he struck down a thousand. So this is said by prolepsis, because this history was written down after all those deeds.

Like tow when it has smelled fire. This is a metaphor from an animate to an inanimate thing, for tow has no sense of smell. It is said as if it were said, "when it has sensed fire". Even the word I used, "sensed", belongs to the same metaphor. But "smelled" was said to convey the speed of it.
And he stretched out his hand and took it. Even if he had not said "he stretched out his hand", we would certainly understand that it was taken with an outstretched hand.
And it was announced to the people of Gaza, saying. He did not say "they announced, saying", or "it was announced by people saying".
If they bind me in seven fresh sinews that have not yet been dried. He did not say "with seven sinews" but "in seven sinews".
If they bind me in seven fresh sinews that have not yet been dried, and I shall become weak. The sentence would be complete even without "and".

And the ambush was sitting for him in the chamber. Some have translated this as "they were besieging", but the Greek has ekathēto [?], that is, "was sitting". This is because "ambush" is singular in Greek, while in Latin one cannot say insidia. The expression needed noting because "the ambush was sitting" was said for those who lay in ambush, for it was they who were sitting.
Now therefore tell me in what you will be bound. He did not say "with what you will be bound" or "by what means you will be bound".
If they bind me in new ropes. He did not say "with ropes".
Likewise: If they bind me in new cords with which no work has been done, and I shall become weak. The sentence would be complete even if "and" were not put before it.
This third you have deceived me. He put "third" (tertium) for "the third time" (tertio) or "three times" (ter). It is a noun for an adverb, which is also often done elegantly in Latin expressions.
Let me be, and I will feel the pillars on which the house is set firm upon them.
